_comment: Hand-authored FAQs per onboarding-spec attribute, keyed by the same attribute path config/attribute_knowledge.json uses. Consumed by scripts/build_docs_reference.py to render the '??? question' blocks under each attribute in docs/reference/json/*. Every attribute in attribute_knowledge.json must have at least four entries covering the four kinds -- omitted, format, performance, edge_case -- and tests/unit/test_attribute_faqs.py fails the build when one is missing, so adding a registry attribute forces its FAQs to be written in the same change. Not loaded by the Spec Builder UI today: the inspector shows purpose/why/tips/errors from attribute_knowledge.json; this file is documentation-only until the app grows a FAQ panel.

kinds.omitted: What happens when the attribute is absent: default, required-error text, or inert.
kinds.format: Quoting, case, shape, prefix, date and three-part-name gotchas.
kinds.performance: Cost or runtime impact, including an explicit 'negligible' when that is true.
kinds.edge_case: Interplay with another attribute, a mode, a load strategy or a platform rule.

@dataflow_group_id.q: What happens if I leave dataflow_group_id out of the spec?
@dataflow_group_id.a: Onboarding hard-rejects the spec: `check_string(spec.get("dataflow_group_id"), "dataflow_group_id", errors, required=True)` fails validation with a missing-field error before any flow is upserted. There is no default; every spec must carry one.

@dataflow_group_id.q: Is there a naming convention or pattern enforced for dataflow_group_id?
@dataflow_group_id.a: The validator only checks it is a non-empty string; there is no regex or pattern constraint. Convention (per docs/00 §1) is a stable business-domain name such as `dfg_finance_txn_ingest`, kept identical across dev and prod rather than encoding the environment.

@dataflow_group_id.q: Does changing dataflow_group_id have any runtime cost?
@dataflow_group_id.a: Not a performance concern but a correctness one: every control-table row is keyed by this id, so it is cheap to change but expensive in effect — see edge_case below. There is no measurable pipeline runtime impact from the id's value itself.

@dataflow_group_id.q: Why do I see duplicate pipelines after I renamed dataflow_group_id and re-ran onboarding?
@dataflow_group_id.a: Re-onboarding upserts rows keyed on this id, so a changed id creates a second, independent set of control-table rows while the original flows under the old id keep running untouched. Fix by restoring the original id or deleting the orphaned rows for the abandoned id.

@dataflow_group_id.q: Can a reconciliation flow use a different dataflow_group_id than the spec root?
@dataflow_group_id.a: Yes — `reconciliation_flows[].dataflow_group_id` is independent and, if absent, defaults to the spec's own root `dataflow_group_id`. Declaring a different one places that recon flow's registration into another group's pipeline instead (V-CYC-4 warns naming both groups). See docs/14 §4.4.

@observability.q: What happens if I omit the observability array entirely?
@observability.a: No telemetry destinations are onboarded and `_validate_observability_destinations` returns an empty list without error. Unlike ingestion/transformation/reconciliation arrays, `observability` deliberately does not count toward the "at least one flow array must be non-empty" rule — it is optional and inert when absent.

@observability.q: Can I write a blank or partially-filled entry in the observability array?
@observability.a: In the Spec Builder UI a wholly blank entry is dropped on save, so it never reaches the JSON spec. A partially-filled entry that does reach the spec (e.g. missing `id` or `type`) fails validation as required fields are missing.

@observability.q: Does adding entries to observability slow down the pipeline update?
@observability.a: Negligible for `triggered` mode — export runs as a separate downstream job task after the pipeline update completes, not inside it. `continuous` mode runs as its own standing pipeline, so it adds no load to the source pipelines either; see docs/08 §1 and §6.

@observability.q: If two destinations reference the same event_log table, is it read twice?
@observability.a: No. `resolve_event_log_tables` de-duplicates the table union across all continuous destinations, so a table named by more than one destination is still read only once into one `@dlt.view`, per docs/08 §2.5.

@observability[].auth.credentials.q: What happens if auth.credentials is left out but auth.type is set to BEARER_TOKEN?
@observability[].auth.credentials.a: `_validate_observability_auth` requires `credentials` as a dict when `auth_type` is `BEARER_TOKEN`, `API_KEY`, or `BASIC_AUTH` — omitting it fails validation via `check_dict(credentials, credentials_path, errors, required=True)`. For `auth.type: NONE` (or no `auth` object at all), `credentials` is not needed.

@observability[].auth.credentials.q: Can I put a plain password or token string directly in auth.credentials?
@observability[].auth.credentials.a: No — every credential value must match `env:<VAR_NAME>` or `secret:<scope>:<key>`; `check_credential_ref` rejects a literal secret value at onboarding time. Resolution happens at dispatch: `env:` reads an environment variable, `secret:` calls `dbutils.secrets.get(scope, key)`. See docs/08 §2.3.

@observability[].auth.credentials.q: Does resolving credentials at every export add noticeable overhead?
@observability[].auth.credentials.a: Negligible — `resolve_credential` is a single env-var read or one `dbutils.secrets.get` call per dispatch, not a per-row operation, so it does not scale with telemetry volume.

@observability[].auth.credentials.q: What if I add an extra key to auth.credentials that a given auth.type does not expect, like a stray field?
@observability[].auth.credentials.a: Keys are written verbatim into the config; an unexpected key is not validated against a strict allowlist inside `credentials` and is silently unused rather than rejected. Only the specific keys each `auth.type` needs (e.g. `token` for `BEARER_TOKEN`) are read by `destination_dispatcher.py::build_auth_headers`.

@observability[].auth.credentials.q: Does auth.credentials apply to a DATABRICKS_VOLUME destination?
@observability[].auth.credentials.a: No — `auth` is ignored entirely for `DATABRICKS_VOLUME`; Volume exports authenticate through native Unity Catalog permissions, not through this block. See docs/08 §2.1.

@observability[].auth.type.q: What is used for auth if I omit the whole auth object?
@observability[].auth.type.a: `build_auth_headers` treats an absent/`None` `auth_config` the same as `type: NONE`: `auth_type = (auth_config or {}).get("type", "NONE")`, so no Authorization header is sent. This is fine for a collector that needs no authentication.

@observability[].auth.type.q: Are the auth.type enum values case-sensitive?
@observability[].auth.type.a: Yes — only the exact uppercase strings `BEARER_TOKEN`, `API_KEY`, `BASIC_AUTH`, `NONE` are accepted by `check_string(..., allowed_values=ALLOWED_OBSERVABILITY_AUTH_TYPES)`; any other casing or value fails onboarding validation.

@observability[].auth.type.q: Does choosing BASIC_AUTH over BEARER_TOKEN cost more per export?
@observability[].auth.type.a: Negligible — `BASIC_AUTH` adds one extra `base64.b64encode` call over a `BEARER_TOKEN` header build; both happen once per dispatch attempt, not per record.

@observability[].auth.type.q: Does auth.type matter for a DATABRICKS_VOLUME destination?
@observability[].auth.type.a: No — the whole `auth` block, including `type`, is ignored for `DATABRICKS_VOLUME` destinations, which rely on Unity Catalog permissions instead. It is only meaningful for `OTLP_CONSUMER`. See docs/08 §2.1.

@observability[].destination_config.comp.q: What compression is used if destination_config.compression is not set?
@observability[].destination_config.comp.a: It defaults to `"none"` per the JSON schema's `observabilityCompression` default, meaning telemetry files are written uncompressed.

@observability[].destination_config.comp.q: Does compression accept the value "NONE" in uppercase?
@observability[].destination_config.comp.a: No — the allowed set is exactly `{"GZIP", "gzip", "none", ""}`; uppercase `"NONE"` is rejected by `check_string(..., allowed_values=ALLOWED_OBSERVABILITY_COMPRESSION)`. Only `"GZIP"`/`"gzip"` enable gzip, and only lowercase `"none"` or an empty string disable it.

@observability[].destination_config.comp.q: Is there a real cost saving from turning on GZIP compression for exported telemetry?
@observability[].destination_config.comp.a: Yes for storage and network transfer of exported files/payloads — gzip typically shrinks JSON/JSONL text significantly — but it is not validated against `file_format`/`type` beyond the enum check itself, so weigh it against CPU spent compressing on every export.

@observability[].destination_config.comp.q: Does the schema restrict compression choices to what a given file_format supports, e.g. is SNAPPY valid for PARQUET here?
@observability[].destination_config.comp.a: No — this framework's `observabilityCompression` enum is only `GZIP`/`gzip`/`none`/`""` for both `DATABRICKS_VOLUME` and `OTLP_CONSUMER`; there is no `SNAPPY` or `PARQUET`-specific compression option, and `file_format` itself only allows `JSONL`/`JSON`. Any claim of PARQUET/SNAPPY support does not match `spec_validator.py` or `onboarding_spec.schema.json`.

@observability[].destination_config.endp.q: What happens if I set type to OTLP_CONSUMER but leave out destination_config.endpoint?
@observability[].destination_config.endp.a: Onboarding rejects the flow: `check_string(endpoint, ..., required=True)` inside `_validate_observability_destination_config` fails because `endpoint` is required whenever `destination_type == "OTLP_CONSUMER"`.

@observability[].destination_config.endp.q: What URL formats are accepted for endpoint?
@observability[].destination_config.endp.a: It must start with `http://` or `https://`; anything else fails with `'{path}.endpoint: must be a full http:// or https:// URL, got ...'`. The schema additionally requires `format: uri`.

@observability[].destination_config.endp.q: Does the endpoint value affect export latency?
@observability[].destination_config.endp.a: Only insofar as network distance/collector load do — the framework itself adds no overhead based on the URL's shape. Use `timeout_ms` and `retry` to bound how long a slow endpoint is allowed to hold up the export.

@observability[].destination_config.endp.q: Do I need destination_config.endpoint for a DATABRICKS_VOLUME destination?
@observability[].destination_config.endp.a: No — Volume exports need only `volume_path`; `endpoint` is meaningful, and required, only for `OTLP_CONSUMER`. See docs/08 §2.2.

@observability[].destination_config.even.q: What happens if mode is continuous but destination_config.event_log_tables is omitted?
@observability[].destination_config.even.a: Onboarding rejects it: `'{path}.destination_config.event_log_tables: is required when mode is 'continuous' -- the continuous observability pipeline has no upstream task to resolve a pipeline from...'`. Without a real spec row, the streaming pipeline falls back at runtime to the pipeline resource's own `dataflow.otel_streaming.event_log_tables` config, or fails with 'there is nothing to stream' if that too is empty (docs/08 §6.1).

@observability[].destination_config.even.q: What format must each entry in event_log_tables use?
@observability[].destination_config.even.a: Each entry must be a fully-qualified, exactly three-part `catalog.schema.table` string (`parts = entry.split("."); len(parts) != 3`). A two-part or unqualified name is rejected per-entry by `_validate_observability_event_log_tables`.

@observability[].destination_config.even.q: Does listing many event_log_tables slow down the continuous pipeline?
@observability[].destination_config.even.a: Each table is a real streaming read that is unioned into `unified_event_log`; more tables means more concurrent streaming sources for that one continuous pipeline. `resolve_event_log_tables` at least de-duplicates the same table named by multiple destinations so it is read only once, per docs/08 §2.5.

@observability[].destination_config.even.q: What happens if I set event_log_tables on a triggered destination?
@observability[].destination_config.even.a: It is rejected: `'only meaningful when mode is 'continuous', but this destination's mode is 'triggered' (the triggered engine resolves its pipeline from the upstream task run)'`. The triggered engine has no use for a fixed table list since it resolves its pipeline dynamically from the run context.

@observability[].destination_config.file.q: What file format is used for Volume exports if file_format is not set?
@observability[].destination_config.file.a: It defaults to `"JSONL"` per the schema's default and docs/08 §2.2 — one JSON object per line, the usual choice for telemetry.

@observability[].destination_config.file.q: What values does file_format actually accept?
@observability[].destination_config.file.a: Only `"JSONL"` or `"JSON"` — `check_string(config.get("file_format"), ..., allowed_values={"JSONL", "JSON"})` for `DATABRICKS_VOLUME`. There is no `PARQUET` option in this schema despite it appearing plausible; do not use it.

@observability[].destination_config.file.q: Is JSONL more efficient than JSON for large telemetry exports?
@observability[].destination_config.file.a: JSONL (one object per line) is generally cheaper to append to and stream-process incrementally than a single JSON array document, which is why docs/08 calls it "the usual choice for telemetry" — but the framework does not measure or enforce this; it is an operational recommendation, not a validated constraint.

@observability[].destination_config.file.q: Does file_format apply to an OTLP_CONSUMER destination?
@observability[].destination_config.file.a: No — `file_format` is read only inside the `DATABRICKS_VOLUME` branch of `_validate_observability_destination_config`; an `OTLP_CONSUMER` destination has no `file_format` field in its schema branch at all (payloads are OTel `ResourceLogs`-shaped, not files).

@observability[].destination_config.prot.q: What protocol is used if I omit destination_config.protocol on an OTLP_CONSUMER destination?
@observability[].destination_config.prot.a: The schema default is `"OTLP_HTTP_JSON"`. The validator itself does not force a default when the key is absent (it only checks the value when present), but the schema and runtime treat missing as `OTLP_HTTP_JSON`.

@observability[].destination_config.prot.q: What exact values does protocol accept, and is it OTLP_HTTP_PROTOBUF or OTLP_HTTP_PROTO?
@observability[].destination_config.prot.a: The allowed values are exactly `OTLP_HTTP_JSON`, `OTLP_HTTP_PROTO`, `OTLP_GRPC` per both `spec_validator.py` and the JSON schema — it is `OTLP_HTTP_PROTO`, not `OTLP_HTTP_PROTOBUF`. Using the wrong spelling fails onboarding validation.

@observability[].destination_config.prot.q: Does choosing OTLP_GRPC instead of OTLP_HTTP_JSON change export throughput?
@observability[].destination_config.prot.a: Not validated at onboarding — the schema comment notes only `OTLP_HTTP_JSON` is actually implemented by `destination_dispatcher.py` today, so any performance difference for `OTLP_HTTP_PROTO`/`OTLP_GRPC` is unverified; treat those as accepted-but-unimplemented and confirm at runtime.

@observability[].destination_config.prot.q: What happens at dispatch time if I set protocol to OTLP_GRPC?
@observability[].destination_config.prot.a: It passes onboarding validation (the value is in the allowed enum) but the schema's own `$comment` states only `OTLP_HTTP_JSON` is implemented by `destination_dispatcher.py` — verify actual dispatch behaviour at runtime since the validator does not check implementation coverage. See docs/08 Extending section.

@observability[].destination_config.reso.q: What happens if resource_attributes is left out?
@observability[].destination_config.reso.a: It defaults to an effectively empty map (`{}` per docs/08 §2.2); only the framework's own built-in resource attributes are attached to exported records, with nothing merged in or overridden.

@observability[].destination_config.reso.q: What value types can resource_attributes hold?
@observability[].destination_config.reso.a: It must be an object whose keys and values are both strings — `check_dict_of_str` enforces this; a non-string value (e.g. a number or nested object) fails validation.

@observability[].destination_config.reso.q: Does adding many resource_attributes slow down each export?
@observability[].destination_config.reso.a: Negligible — they are merged once per `ResourceLogs` entry by `destination_dispatcher.py::merge_resource_attributes` immediately before dispatch, a cheap dict merge, not a per-record loop.

@observability[].destination_config.reso.q: What happens if a key in resource_attributes has a typo or duplicates a framework-built attribute?
@observability[].destination_config.reso.a: A typo'd key is written verbatim and simply becomes an extra, unused attribute — it is not validated against any known set. A key matching a framework-built attribute name overrides it, since `merge_resource_attributes` merges the spec's values in, taking precedence over same-named keys the framework already built.

@observability[].destination_config.volu.q: What happens if type is DATABRICKS_VOLUME and volume_path is omitted?
@observability[].destination_config.volu.a: Onboarding rejects the flow via `check_string(volume_path, ..., required=True)`. At runtime, if a misconfiguration somehow reaches the continuous engine, docs/08 §6.2 notes a continuous Volume destination missing `volume_path` is instead skipped with a WARNING rather than failing the whole pipeline update.

@observability[].destination_config.volu.q: What prefix must volume_path use, and can I use a ${param} placeholder in it?
@observability[].destination_config.volu.a: It must start with `/Volumes/` — `'{path}.volume_path: must start with \'/Volumes/\', got ...'` otherwise. Unlike other path fields, `transformation/parameters.py` deliberately excludes `destination_config.volume_path` from `${param}` substitution, since a `${param}`-prefixed value would newly fail the strict `/Volumes/` check — write the literal path instead.

@observability[].destination_config.volu.q: Does the choice of Volume path affect export performance?
@observability[].destination_config.volu.a: Negligible from the framework's side — it is a plain Unity Catalog Volume write; any performance difference would come from the underlying storage/volume characteristics, not from anything this attribute controls.

@observability[].destination_config.volu.q: Is volume_path required for an OTLP_CONSUMER destination too?
@observability[].destination_config.volu.a: No — `volume_path` is only checked inside the `DATABRICKS_VOLUME` branch of `_validate_observability_destination_config`; an `OTLP_CONSUMER` destination uses `endpoint` instead and needs no Volume path at all.

@observability[].enabled.q: If I don't set observability[].enabled, is the destination active or not?
@observability[].enabled.a: It defaults to `true` — the schema's default is `true` and omitting the attribute is not the same as setting it `false`. A destination is active unless explicitly disabled.

@observability[].enabled.q: Does enabled accept anything besides a plain boolean, like the string "true"?
@observability[].enabled.a: No — `check_bool` requires an actual JSON boolean; a string like `"true"` fails validation. Use `true`/`false` literals.

@observability[].enabled.q: Is there any cost to leaving a destination in the spec with enabled: false?
@observability[].enabled.a: Negligible — a disabled destination is dropped entirely by `config_loader.py`'s `parse_config_rows` (`if not row.get("enabled", False): continue`), so callers never see it and no export runs for it; it only occupies a row in `observability_config`.

@observability[].enabled.q: How is a disabled destination reported — as an error, a skip, or silently?
@observability[].enabled.a: Silently, by design — the doc explicitly notes there is no "enabled" flag callers must remember to check, because `config_loader.py` filters it out before any consumer sees it; it is not logged as an error or a skip event.

@observability[].id.q: What happens if I leave out observability[].id?
@observability[].id.a: Onboarding rejects the destination: `check_string(destination_id, f"{label}.id", errors, required=True)` fails since `id` has no default and is always required.

@observability[].id.q: Are there naming rules for observability[].id beyond being non-empty?
@observability[].id.a: The schema only requires a string with `minLength: 1`; there is no pattern constraint, but the id becomes `destination_id` in `observability_config`, so a stable, descriptive name like `dest-otlp-example` is recommended.

@observability[].id.q: Does the id value have any runtime performance implication?
@observability[].id.a: None directly — it is purely a lookup key. Its only operational effect is on how re-onboarding behaves (see edge_case).

@observability[].id.q: What happens if two destinations in the same spec share the same id?
@observability[].id.a: Onboarding rejects it: `'{label}.id: '<id>' is already used by observability[<n>] -- destination id must be unique within a spec'`. Re-onboarding the same `id` for the same dataflow group instead upserts (MERGEs) the same row rather than duplicating it, per docs/08 §2.1.

@observability[].mode.q: What mode does a destination run in if mode is not specified?
@observability[].mode.a: It resolves to `"triggered"` everywhere — both the schema default and `config_loader.py`'s defensive `row.get("mode") or DEFAULT_DESTINATION_MODE` read — so a pre-v1.3.0 `observability_config` row with no `mode` column value keeps working with no migration needed.

@observability[].mode.q: What are the exact accepted values for mode?
@observability[].mode.a: Only `"triggered"` or `"continuous"` — `check_string(..., allowed_values=ALLOWED_OBSERVABILITY_MODES)`; any other string fails onboarding validation.

@observability[].mode.q: Is continuous mode more expensive to run than triggered?
@observability[].mode.a: Yes in kind, not just degree — `triggered` runs once per pipeline update as a bounded job task, while `continuous` is a standing, always-on Lakeflow pipeline streaming event logs continuously, so it consumes compute even when no source pipeline is currently updating. See docs/08 §1.

@observability[].mode.q: Can the same destination_id be served by both triggered and continuous mode at once?
@observability[].mode.a: No — `mode` is exactly what stops one destination being served, and therefore double-exported, by both observability engines; each destination is served by exactly one of the two. See docs/08 §2.1.

@observability[].retry.backoff_multiplie.q: What backoff_multiplier is used if I don't set it?
@observability[].retry.backoff_multiplie.a: It defaults to `2.0` per the schema and `_validate_observability_retry`'s implicit default; exponential backoff doubles the delay between retry attempts unless overridden.

@observability[].retry.backoff_multiplie.q: What values are rejected for backoff_multiplier?
@observability[].retry.backoff_multiplie.a: It must be a number strictly greater than 1 and not a boolean — the validator explicitly checks `isinstance(backoff_multiplier, bool) or not isinstance(..., (int, float)) or backoff_multiplier <= 1` and errors `'must be a number > 1, got ...'` otherwise. `1.0` or lower is rejected.

@observability[].retry.backoff_multiplie.q: Does a high backoff_multiplier make failed exports take much longer to give up?
@observability[].retry.backoff_multiplie.a: Yes — combined with `retry.max_attempts`, a larger multiplier grows the delay between attempts exponentially, though docs/08 §2.4 notes the computed delay is capped at 30s per attempt, bounding the worst case.

@observability[].retry.backoff_multiplie.q: Does backoff_multiplier apply to a DATABRICKS_VOLUME destination?
@observability[].retry.backoff_multiplie.a: No — `retry` (including `backoff_multiplier`) is documented as `OTLP_CONSUMER` only in docs/08 §2.1; a Volume export has no network retry loop to back off.

@observability[].retry.max_attempts.q: How many retries happen if max_attempts is not set?
@observability[].retry.max_attempts.a: It defaults to `3` — both the schema default and `destination_dispatcher.py`'s `DEFAULT_MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3` used via `retry_config.get("max_attempts", DEFAULT_MAX_ATTEMPTS)`.

@observability[].retry.max_attempts.q: Is there an upper bound on max_attempts, and does the validator enforce it?
@observability[].retry.max_attempts.a: The JSON schema caps it at `maximum: 10`, but `spec_validator.py`'s `_validate_observability_retry` only checks `check_int(..., minimum=1)` — it does not enforce the upper bound. A value of 1 is the floor; values above 10 are not rejected at onboarding by the Python validator even though the schema disallows them, so validate against both gates.

@observability[].retry.max_attempts.q: Does setting max_attempts high risk long-running or stuck exports?
@observability[].retry.max_attempts.a: Yes — more attempts combined with exponential `backoff_multiplier` (capped at 30s per attempt per docs/08 §2.4) extends the worst-case time before an export gives up; retried status codes are `429, 500, 502, 503, 504`.

@observability[].retry.max_attempts.q: Does max_attempts apply to a DATABRICKS_VOLUME destination?
@observability[].retry.max_attempts.a: No — like `backoff_multiplier`, `retry.max_attempts` is documented as `OTLP_CONSUMER` only; Volume writes have no network retry loop.

@observability[].timeout_ms.q: What request timeout applies if timeout_ms is omitted?
@observability[].timeout_ms.a: It defaults to `5000` (5 seconds) — `destination_dispatcher.py`'s `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS = 5000`, read via `retry_config.get("timeout_ms", DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS)`.

@observability[].timeout_ms.q: Where does timeout_ms sit in the spec — nested under retry or at the destination top level?
@observability[].timeout_ms.a: It sits at the destination's top level, a sibling of `retry`, not nested inside it — but it is folded into `retry_config_json` for storage by `upsert_observability_config`. Get the nesting wrong (e.g. inside `retry`) and it will not be read as `timeout_ms`.

@observability[].timeout_ms.q: Does raising timeout_ms help with a slow OTLP collector?
@observability[].timeout_ms.a: Yes, that is its purpose — docs/08's troubleshooting table for `destination_outage` (network timeout / HTTP 503 / ConnectionTimeout) suggests checking collector health and increasing `timeout_ms` / `retry.max_attempts` together.

@observability[].timeout_ms.q: Does timeout_ms apply to a DATABRICKS_VOLUME destination?
@observability[].timeout_ms.a: No — per docs/08 §2.1, `timeout_ms` is 'Not applicable to Volume exports'; it is only meaningful for `OTLP_CONSUMER` network calls.

@observability[].type.q: What happens if I omit observability[].type?
@observability[].type.a: Onboarding rejects the destination: `check_string(destination_type, f"{label}.type", errors, required=True, allowed_values=...)` fails since `type` has no default and is always required.

@observability[].type.q: What are the exact accepted values for type?
@observability[].type.a: Only `"DATABRICKS_VOLUME"` or `"OTLP_CONSUMER"` — `ALLOWED_OBSERVABILITY_DESTINATION_TYPES = {"DATABRICKS_VOLUME", "OTLP_CONSUMER"}`; any other string fails validation.

@observability[].type.q: Is one destination type more expensive than the other?
@observability[].type.a: Not validated as a performance concern by the framework — `DATABRICKS_VOLUME` writes files to Unity Catalog storage while `OTLP_CONSUMER` makes network calls with retry/timeout overhead; the relevant cost knobs (`retry`, `timeout_ms`) exist only for `OTLP_CONSUMER`.

@observability[].type.q: Does type determine which destination_config fields are required?
@observability[].type.a: Yes — `type` drives conditional requirements in both the schema's `allOf`/`if`/`then` blocks and `_validate_observability_destination_config`: `DATABRICKS_VOLUME` requires `volume_path`, `OTLP_CONSUMER` requires `endpoint`. Getting `type` wrong means the wrong set of required fields is enforced.

@observability_enabled.q: What happens in the generated spec if observability_enabled is left off in the Spec Builder?
@observability_enabled.a: This is a Spec Builder UI-only helper, not a real onboarding-spec key (`emit: "never"` in `databricks-app/config/registry/observability.json`) — when off, the `observability` array is omitted from the emitted spec entirely and no telemetry is exported. It never appears in the actual JSON sent to onboarding.

@observability_enabled.q: Will observability_enabled: true ever appear as a literal key in my onboarding spec JSON?
@observability_enabled.a: No — it is a boolean toggle local to the Spec Builder (`server/core/serializer.py`/`deserializer.py` read and set it only on the in-memory builder document), used purely to decide whether to render the Destinations section and whether to emit the real `observability` array; `spec_validator.py` has no `ALLOWED_ROOT_KEYS` entry for it.

@observability_enabled.q: Does toggling observability_enabled in the Builder cost anything at pipeline runtime?
@observability_enabled.a: Negligible — it only controls Builder-side visibility and whether `observability` is emitted; it has no runtime code path of its own since it never reaches the spec or the validator.

@observability_enabled.q: What happens if I turn observability_enabled off after already adding destinations in the Builder?
@observability_enabled.a: Per `Builder.jsx`, the emitted spec only includes `observability` when `observability_enabled === true` (`if(obs.length && r.v["@observability_enabled"]===true) out.observability=obs`); turning it off drops the whole array from the generated spec even if destination entries are still filled in the UI, so re-enabling it before saving is required to keep them.

@pipeline_parameters.q: What happens to ${param} placeholders if pipeline_parameters is omitted?
@pipeline_parameters.a: `pipeline_parameters` defaults to `{}` (docs/00 §1); any `${param}` placeholder in `transformation_sql`, `filter_condition` or path fields then has no matching key, and `substitute_dynamic_parameters`/`substitute_path_parameters` raise `FrameworkConfigError` for an undefined placeholder — this is checked at onboarding time by `_validate_path_parameters`/`_validate_sql_syntax`.

@pipeline_parameters.q: Do I need to add quotes around a string pipeline_parameters value inside my SQL?
@pipeline_parameters.a: No — string values are automatically single-quoted during substitution; wrapping a placeholder in your own quotes (`'${region_code}'`) produces a doubled-quote literal (`''EMEA''`) and a `ParseException` at runtime. Write `region = ${region_code}` unquoted, per docs/03 §5.

@pipeline_parameters.q: Does changing pipeline_parameters require re-onboarding, and is that expensive?
@pipeline_parameters.a: No re-onboarding is needed — unlike `{{catalog}}`/`{{env}}` template variables (resolved once at onboarding), `${param}` values are resolved fresh on every pipeline update by editing `pipeline_parameters` and re-running, per docs/03 §5's comparison table.

@pipeline_parameters.q: Can pipeline_parameters be used inside observability destination_config.volume_path?
@pipeline_parameters.a: No — `transformation/parameters.py` deliberately excludes `observability_config.destination_config.volume_path` from path-parameter substitution, since a `${param}`-prefixed value would newly fail the strict `/Volumes/`-prefix check at onboarding; it is left out of scope rather than half-supported.

@spark_config.q: What Spark settings apply if spark_config is left out of the spec?
@spark_config.a: Only the framework's built-in defaults apply — as of the documented contract, `FRAMEWORK_SPARK_DEFAULTS` in `engine/spark_config.py` carries exactly one entry, `{"spark.sql.shuffle.partitions": "200"}`, restating Spark's own default explicitly. No group-scoped overrides are applied.

@spark_config.q: Can spark_config values be nested objects, or must a key start with a specific prefix?
@spark_config.a: Every key must be a string starting with `"spark."`, and every value must be a `str`/`int`/`float`/`bool` — a dict or list value, or a key without the `spark.` prefix, is rejected by `_validate_spark_config` with e.g. `'{path}.{key}: expected a Spark configuration key ... got ... -- keys must start with 'spark.''`. Values are rendered with plain `str()` before `spark.conf.set` (booleans as lowercase `true`/`false`), so a numeric value like `200` is stored as the string `"200"`.

@spark_config.q: Can spark_config actually change pipeline performance, e.g. shuffle partitions?
@spark_config.a: Yes — it is applied via `spark.conf.set` on the pipeline session before any flow is registered, so every `@dlt.table`/`@dlt.view` closure subsequently defined executes under it; e.g. `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` genuinely changes shuffle parallelism for the whole group.

@spark_config.q: Does a value in spark_config always win over the pipeline resource's own dataflow.spark.conf setting?
@spark_config.a: No — precedence is the opposite: this is the middle of a three-layer chain (`FRAMEWORK_SPARK_DEFAULTS` < `spark_config` < the pipeline resource's own `dataflow.spark.conf`), so the pipeline resource's bundle-level setting overrides `spark_config` per-key, not the reverse; resolution is a per-key merge, never a wholesale replace. See docs/01 §5.

@spark_config.q: Should I ever put pipelines.incompatibleViewCheck.enabled=false into spark_config to work around a streaming-view read error?
@spark_config.a: No — docs/13 explicitly records this as evaluated and rejected: it is pipeline-wide (disables the guard for every dataset in the group via `engine/spark_config.py`) and does not make a genuinely streaming plan batch-readable, it only silences the check. See docs/13 (L4 streaming-view section).

compare_columns.q: What happens if compare_columns is left empty or unset?
compare_columns.a: It defaults to key-presence-only matching: every key present on both sides counts as matched regardless of other column values. `__framework_hash_value` is NULL throughout, and `matcher.py` forces `hash_equal = True` when the list is empty.

compare_columns.q: Is compare_columns entered as a JSON array or a comma-separated string?
compare_columns.a: In the onboarding UI it is entered as a comma-separated list, but it is written to the spec as a JSON array of strings, e.g. `["amount", "status"]`.

compare_columns.q: Does listing more compare_columns increase join cost?
compare_columns.a: No -- they are folded into a single `__framework_hash_value` SHA-256 digest (columns alphabetically sorted), so the join itself stays a single-column comparison regardless of how many columns are listed; the cost is one extra hash computation pass, not a wider join.

Yes -- when `hash_precomputed` is `true`, `compare_columns` is not hashed at all here; the side's stored `__framework_hash_value` is trusted verbatim, so it must already have been computed over the same resolved, alphabetically-sorted column set this flow declares, or drift will be silently misreported. See docs/07 section 9.

dataflow_group_id.q: What happens if I leave dataflow_group_id unset on a reconciliation flow?
dataflow_group_id.a: It defaults to the spec's own top-level `dataflow_group_id` -- the common case. It stays optional under `execution_mode: job`, where the standalone engine handles the group-less case, but onboarding rejects it as required once `execution_mode` is `pipeline` or `pipeline_audit_only` (V-CYC-6): 'is required when execution_mode is ... a group-less reconciliation flow has no Lakeflow pipeline to be registered into'.

dataflow_group_id.q: Is dataflow_group_id the same value as the spec's top-level dataflow_group_id?
dataflow_group_id.a: Usually yes -- omitting the flow-level key inherits the spec's own top-level `dataflow_group_id`. Naming a different value registers this flow inside that OTHER group's Lakeflow pipeline update instead, which is the supported way to reconcile against or heal into tables another group owns. It is a plain string, not a three-part name.

dataflow_group_id.q: Does pointing dataflow_group_id at another group cost anything extra?
dataflow_group_id.a: It changes where compute runs, not how much. The flow's L3-L5 nodes get registered in that other group's pipeline update rather than this spec's own, so that pipeline pays the extra scan/join cost described in docs/07 section 11.6 instead of this one.

dataflow_group_id.q: What happens if I switch a job-mode flow to pipeline mode but a job resource still runs a reconciliation task for the same reconciliation_id?
dataflow_group_id.a: The reconciliation runs twice per cycle -- once inside the pipeline update (via dataflow_group_id) and once as the standalone job task -- and each pass appends its own corrections into `append_target_table`. Remove the job task, or keep `execution_mode: job`. See docs/13 R8.

dataflow_id.q: What happens if I forget dataflow_id on an ingestion flow?
dataflow_id.a: Onboarding rejects the flow with 'is required but was missing or empty' against `ingestion_flow[<unknown>].dataflow_id`. The flow label itself falls back to `<missing dataflow_id>` in the error, so fix the first flow listed first.

dataflow_id.q: Can dataflow_id contain spaces or dots like a table name?
dataflow_id.a: It is validated only as a non-empty string; there is no pattern restriction in `spec_validator.py`. Keep it identifier-like anyway since it is used verbatim to build the source-plane consumer id `f"{dataflow_id}:source"`.

dataflow_id.q: Does the length or format of dataflow_id affect pipeline runtime?
dataflow_id.a: Negligible. It is only used as a lookup key and DAG-node/consumer-id string, never used in a data-shaping expression or scan.

dataflow_id.q: How does a transformation flow actually reference an ingestion flow's dataflow_id?
dataflow_id.a: A transformation flow reads it via `source_inputs[].table` (the qualified target the ingestion flow published), not by naming `dataflow_id` directly in the referencing flow. `dataflow_id` is required on both ingestion and transformation flows, but transformation flows also carry their own `flow_step_id`. See docs/00_master_reference_index.md.

decrypted_columns.q: What happens when a source_inputs entry has no decrypted_columns?
decrypted_columns.a: Nothing is decrypted: `_validate_decrypted_columns` returns when the list is absent, and the input view exposes ciphertext columns as stored. Add the list only for columns the SQL must read in clear.

decrypted_columns.q: Where in the spec may decrypted_columns appear?
decrypted_columns.a: Only inside a `source_inputs[]` entry of a transformation flow. It is not a `target_config` key and not an ingestion attribute; the schema and `ALLOWED_SOURCE_INPUT_KEYS` allow it in that one place.

One `aes_decrypt` plus a cast per row per listed column, applied on the input view before the SQL runs. The key is resolved once per flow. Cost scales with rows times columns listed, so decrypt only what the SQL needs.

decrypted_columns.q: Does the decrypted plaintext get written anywhere?
decrypted_columns.a: Only if your `transformation_sql` selects it into the target. The overlay lives on the input view inside the pipeline graph; re-encrypt on the target with `target_config.encrypted_columns` if the output must stay protected.

decrypted_columns[].cast_to_type.q: Can I leave cast_to_type out and let Spark infer the type?
decrypted_columns[].cast_to_type.a: No. It is `required=True`: `...cast_to_type: is required but was missing or empty`. `aes_decrypt` returns binary, so the framework needs the target type to cast to.

decrypted_columns[].cast_to_type.q: What values does cast_to_type accept, and is case significant?
decrypted_columns[].cast_to_type.a: Any Spark SQL type string such as `string`, `int`, `decimal(18,2)` or `timestamp`. It is compared case-insensitively against the encrypted column's `original_data_type` tag, so `STRING` and `string` are equal.
Negligible against the decrypt: `.cast(cast_to_type)` is a per-row conversion of the already decrypted string.

decrypted_columns[].cast_to_type.q: What if cast_to_type disagrees with how the column was encrypted?
decrypted_columns[].cast_to_type.a: The update fails at graph definition with `decrypted_columns cast_to_type mismatch for column '<name>': configured cast_to_type='int' but the encrypted column's tagged original_data_type is 'string'`. The tag comes from the producer's `source_data_type` declaration or the type Spark observed at encryption time.

decrypted_columns[].column_name.q: Is column_name required on a decrypted column?
decrypted_columns[].column_name.a: Yes: `...decrypted_columns[<n>].column_name: is required but was missing or empty`. It names the ciphertext column in the input table.

decrypted_columns[].column_name.q: Which name goes here, the original column or the encrypted output column?
decrypted_columns[].column_name.a: The column as it exists in the input table, which is the producer's `encrypted_columns[].output_column` (or its `column_name` when it was encrypted in place). It must pass `assert_safe_identifier` at run time.

decrypted_columns[].column_name.q: Does naming a column that is not encrypted cost anything?
decrypted_columns[].column_name.a: It fails rather than costs: `aes_decrypt` on plaintext raises inside the pipeline and the update fails. Not validated at onboarding.

decrypted_columns[].column_name.q: What if the column is missing from the input table?
decrypted_columns[].column_name.a: Graph definition fails with `Column '<name>' configured for decryption not present in DataFrame`, wrapped in a `CryptoError`. Onboarding cannot see the input schema, so this surfaces only at run time.

decrypted_columns[].input_name.q: Do I need input_name inside a decrypted column?
decrypted_columns[].input_name.a: No. In the spec a decrypted column is nested under the `source_inputs[]` entry it belongs to, so the input is implied. The Spec Builder shows `input_name` here only to attach the row to its parent input.

decrypted_columns[].input_name.q: What happens if I hand-write input_name inside a decrypted column?
decrypted_columns[].input_name.a: The JSON-schema gate rejects it: `decryptedColumn` has `additionalProperties: false` and no such key. The Python validator does not check unknown keys inside `decrypted_columns`, so validate against the schema too.

decrypted_columns[].input_name.q: Does this helper affect the pipeline?
decrypted_columns[].input_name.a: No. It never reaches the spec or the control table.

decrypted_columns[].input_name.q: How do I decrypt the same column from two different inputs?
decrypted_columns[].input_name.a: Declare a `decrypted_columns` entry under each `source_inputs[]` entry. Each input view gets its own overlay; nothing is shared between inputs.

decrypted_columns[].mode.q: Which cipher mode is used when mode is omitted on decryption?
decrypted_columns[].mode.a: `GCM`, the same default the encryption side uses (`col_config.get("mode", "GCM")`). If the producer encrypted with `CBC` or `ECB`, you must say so here.
Yes: the validator accepts exactly `GCM`, `CBC` or `ECB` for the encryption side, and the runtime passes the string straight to `aes_decrypt`. Write it in upper case.

decrypted_columns[].mode.q: Is one mode faster to decrypt than another?
decrypted_columns[].mode.a: Differences are small next to I/O. GCM additionally verifies the authentication tag; CBC and ECB do not. None of them is a reason to pick a mode over its security properties.

decrypted_columns[].mode.q: What happens when the decryption mode does not match the encryption mode?
decrypted_columns[].mode.a: `aes_decrypt` fails or returns garbage and the update fails inside the pipeline; onboarding cannot detect it because the two sides live in different flows. Keep mode identical on both `encrypted_columns[]` and `decrypted_columns[]` for the same column.

decrypted_columns[].output_column.q: What happens if I omit output_column on a decrypted column?
decrypted_columns[].output_column.a: The plaintext replaces the ciphertext column in place: `output_column` defaults to `column_name` in `apply_aes_column_decryption`. Set it to keep both.

decrypted_columns[].output_column.q: Are there naming rules for output_column?
decrypted_columns[].output_column.a: It must be a safe identifier (`assert_safe_identifier`): letters, digits and underscores. Onboarding checks only that it is a string; an unsafe name fails at graph definition.

decrypted_columns[].output_column.q: Does writing to a new output_column cost more than in-place?
decrypted_columns[].output_column.a: Marginally: the view carries one extra column. The decrypt itself is identical.

decrypted_columns[].output_column.q: Can output_column collide with a column the SQL already uses?
decrypted_columns[].output_column.a: Yes, silently: `withColumn` overwrites an existing column of that name on the input view before the SQL runs. Choose a distinct name such as `<column>_plain`.

decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_catalo.q: Is secret_catalog required for a decrypted column?
decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_catalo.a: Yes. `check_secret_ref` requires all three of `secret_catalog`, `secret_schema` and `secret_key`; a missing part reports `...secret.secret_catalog: is required but was missing or empty`.

decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_catalo.q: Is this a Unity Catalog catalog or a classic secret scope?
decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_catalo.a: A Unity Catalog three-level secret: the runtime resolves `dbutils.secrets.get(catalog=, schema=, key=)`. Classic workspace scopes are not supported anywhere in the framework.

decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_catalo.q: Is the key fetched per row?
decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_catalo.a: No. `resolve_secret_ref` runs once per column config at graph definition; the resolved key is a literal in the decrypt expression.

decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_catalo.q: Can the decryption secret live in a different catalog from the encryption secret?
decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_catalo.a: Yes, as long as both resolve to the same key bytes. Use the same reference on both sides to avoid rotation drift.

decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_key.q: What error appears when secret_key is missing?
decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_key.a: `...secret.secret_key: is required but was missing or empty` at onboarding.

decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_key.q: Does the value here hold the key material?
decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_key.a: No. It is the name of the secret; the bytes are read from Unity Catalog at graph definition. A literal key in the spec would be stored in plain text in the control table, and the Spec Builder refuses keys named like secrets.

decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_key.q: Does the key length affect decrypt speed?
decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_key.a: Negligibly. Spark's `aes_decrypt` accepts 16, 24 or 32-byte keys; throughput differences between them are dwarfed by I/O.

decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_key.q: After rotating the key, what happens to rows encrypted with the old one?
decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_key.a: They no longer decrypt: `aes_decrypt` with the wrong key fails the update. Rotate by re-encrypting the source column, then switch both `encrypted_columns[]` and `decrypted_columns[]` references together. See docs/05 §5.

decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_schema.q: What if secret_schema is left out?
decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_schema.a: Onboarding rejects the column: `...secret.secret_schema: is required but was missing or empty`.

decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_schema.q: Should the schema name be quoted or qualified?
decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_schema.a: A bare schema name, e.g. `security`; the catalog is the sibling `secret_catalog` key. Case is passed through as written.

decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_schema.q: Does the schema choice change anything at run time?
decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_schema.a: No; it is one component of a single lookup made once per column.

decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_schema.q: What happens when the pipeline's run-as identity cannot read the secret?
decrypted_columns[].secret.secret_schema.a: Onboarding cannot check grants; the first update fails at graph definition when `dbutils.secrets.get` is denied. Grant the pipeline principal access to the secret before running.

dq_config.quarantine_table.q: What happens if I don't set dq_config.quarantine_table at all?
dq_config.quarantine_table.a: No quarantine table is registered. If a rule still uses `action: "quarantine"`, those rows have nowhere to go; the validator does not cross-check this today, so the failure surfaces only at pipeline registration/runtime, not at onboarding.

dq_config.quarantine_table.q: Is quarantine_table a full three-part name or just a suffix?
dq_config.quarantine_table.a: It is a plain string table name, validated only as a non-empty string by `check_string`. The sample convention is `<target_table>_quarantine`; it is not auto-derived, so you must spell it out yourself.

dq_config.quarantine_table.q: Does naming a quarantine table cost anything if no rule ever quarantines a row?
dq_config.quarantine_table.a: Negligible. `_validate_dq_config` in `spec_validator.py` explicitly notes a `quarantine_table` name with no `action: "quarantine"` rule is accepted, not an error — it just produces no table, flagged only as a `logger.warning`-worthy no-op.

dq_config.quarantine_table.q: I set quarantine_table but rows still aren't landing anywhere — why?
dq_config.quarantine_table.a: The quarantine sibling table is only registered when at least one rule in `dq_config.rules` has `action: "quarantine"` (see `dq/quarantine.py::register_main_and_quarantine_tables`). A `warn`/`drop`/`fail`-only rule set means `quarantine_table` is configured but inert.

dq_config.record_id_column.q: What is written to __framework_record_id if record_id_column is not set?
dq_config.record_id_column.a: `NULL` for every quarantined row. `dq/quarantine.py` fills `__framework_record_id` from `record_id_column` when configured and present on the DataFrame, else `NULL` — it never errors for its absence.

dq_config.record_id_column.q: Does record_id_column need to be a unique/primary key column?
dq_config.record_id_column.a: No — it is just a string column name, validated only as a non-empty string (`check_string`). It is meant for traceability, not uniqueness enforcement, so any column that helps you find the source record is fine.

dq_config.record_id_column.q: Does adding record_id_column slow down quarantine processing?
dq_config.record_id_column.a: Negligible — it is a single extra column lookup added alongside the other diagnostic fields (`__framework_quarantine_timestamp_utc`, failed-rule ids) already being written to quarantined rows.

dq_config.record_id_column.q: What if the column named in record_id_column doesn't exist on the incoming DataFrame?
dq_config.record_id_column.a: It resolves to `NULL` on `__framework_record_id` rather than failing — `dq/quarantine.py` only populates the value "when configured and present on the DataFrame", so a typo'd column name degrades silently rather than erroring.

dq_config.rules.q: What happens if dq_config.rules is left empty or omitted?
dq_config.rules.a: No expectations are evaluated at all — every row passes through untouched. This is a valid, inert configuration, not an error.

dq_config.rules.q: Is rules a JSON array or a keyed object of rule definitions?
dq_config.rules.a: Always a JSON array of objects: `"rules": [{...}, {...}]`. `_validate_dq_config` explicitly checks `isinstance(rules, list)` and errors with 'expected a list of DQ rule objects' otherwise.

dq_config.rules.q: Does adding many DQ rules meaningfully slow down a pipeline update?
dq_config.rules.a: Each rule becomes one Lakeflow expectation evaluated per row, so cost scales roughly linearly with rule count — for typical rule counts (single digits) this is negligible next to the read/write cost of the flow itself; not separately benchmarked in this repo.

dq_config.rules.q: Can one rule set both drop and quarantine behaviour for the same condition?
dq_config.rules.a: No — each rule object has exactly one `action`. To both drop obviously-bad rows and quarantine borderline ones, write two separate rules with different `expression`s, each carrying its own `action`.

dq_config.rules.q: What happens if a rule's action is fail and the condition triggers mid-run?
dq_config.rules.a: The whole pipeline update aborts and the target transaction rolls back — see docs/04 Data Quality Actions table. Reserve `fail` for genuinely unrecoverable conditions; downgrade to `drop` or `quarantine` otherwise.

dq_config.rules[].action.q: What error do I get if a rule is missing its action?
dq_config.rules[].action.a: Onboarding rejects the flow: `check_string` is called with `required=True`, producing '<path>.action: is required but was missing or empty'. There is no default action.

dq_config.rules[].action.q: Are the action values case-sensitive, e.g. can I write WARN or Quarantine?
dq_config.rules[].action.a: Yes, case-sensitive — `ALLOWED_DQ_ACTIONS = {"warn", "drop", "fail", "quarantine"}` is an exact-match set checked via `check_string(..., allowed_values=...)`. `"WARN"` is rejected as not in the allowed set.

dq_config.rules[].action.q: Is any one action (warn/drop/fail/quarantine) noticeably more expensive than the others?
dq_config.rules[].action.a: Negligible difference — all four evaluate the same per-row boolean `expression`; `quarantine` additionally forks the stream to write a second table (`dq/quarantine.py`), which is the one action with a real extra I/O cost, though still proportional to failing-row volume, not total volume.

dq_config.rules[].action.q: If I use action: quarantine but never configured quarantine_table, what happens?
dq_config.rules[].action.a: Onboarding does not cross-validate this — the flow still validates. At runtime the quarantine sibling table registration depends on `dq_config.quarantine_table` being set; per docs/04 'Errors' guidance, quarantined rows effectively go nowhere without it.

dq_config.rules[].expression.q: What happens if a rule's expression is left blank?
dq_config.rules[].expression.a: Onboarding rejects the flow with '<path>.expression: is required but was missing or empty', since `check_string` is called with `required=True`.

dq_config.rules[].expression.q: Can expression reference {{catalog}} or {{env}} template placeholders?
dq_config.rules[].expression.a: Yes — the attribute inspector's tip confirms `expression` supports `{{catalog}}` and `{{env}}` template variables, resolved at onboarding time, the same mechanism documented in docs/03 §5 Parameter Substitution.

dq_config.rules[].expression.q: Does a complex SQL expression in a DQ rule slow the pipeline down noticeably?
dq_config.rules[].expression.a: It runs as a per-row boolean Spark SQL predicate alongside the rest of the flow's transformations, so cost is proportional to expression complexity times row count — negligible for simple comparisons, but a heavy subquery-style expression would not be typical or recommended here.

dq_config.rules[].expression.q: Will expression be validated for correct SQL syntax at onboarding time?
dq_config.rules[].expression.a: No — `spec_validator.py` only checks it is a non-empty string (`check_string`); it does not parse or execute the SQL. A malformed expression is only caught when the pipeline actually runs it as a Lakeflow expectation.

dq_config.rules[].rule_id.q: What happens if rule_id is missing from a DQ rule?
dq_config.rules[].rule_id.a: Onboarding rejects the flow: '<path>.rule_id: is required but was missing or empty', since `check_string` runs with `required=True`.

dq_config.rules[].rule_id.q: Does rule_id need to follow a particular naming convention like a prefix?
dq_config.rules[].rule_id.a: No format is enforced beyond being a non-empty string. The reference sample uses a `dq_`-prefixed convention (`dq_amount_non_negative`) for readability, but this is a convention, not a validated rule.

dq_config.rules[].rule_id.q: Does rule_id itself have any runtime cost?
dq_config.rules[].rule_id.a: None — it is purely an identifier used for traceability, not evaluated as part of the DQ logic.

dq_config.rules[].rule_id.q: What happens if two rules in the same dq_config.rules list share the same rule_id?
dq_config.rules[].rule_id.a: Not validated at onboarding — `_validate_dq_config` does not check uniqueness across the list. Since `rule_id` is what appears in `__framework_dq_failed_rule_ids`, a duplicate makes quarantine diagnostics ambiguous about which rule actually failed; verify at runtime.

error_handling.on_failure.q: What happens if error_handling.on_failure is not set?
error_handling.on_failure.a: It defaults to `fail`, per the JSON schema description ('Default: 'fail'. Evaluated per target.'). A target's reconciliation failure propagates and stops the run.

error_handling.on_failure.q: What are the only legal values for error_handling.on_failure?
error_handling.on_failure.a: `fail` or `warn` -- `ALLOWED_RECONCILIATION_FAILURE_MODES = {"fail", "warn"}`; any other value fails the allowed-values check.

error_handling.on_failure.q: Does setting on_failure to warn cost more at runtime?
error_handling.on_failure.a: Negligible -- `warn` just logs the failure and writes a FAILED `reconciliation_run_log` row for that target instead of raising, then continues to the next target. It avoids re-running already-succeeded targets on retry, which can save cost versus `fail` aborting the whole run.

error_handling.on_failure.q: Does error_handling.on_failure behave the same in pipeline mode as in job mode?
error_handling.on_failure.a: The try/except semantics are unchanged, but the blast radius is not: in job mode `fail` fails only that job task, while in pipeline mode re-raising fails that flow and therefore the whole pipeline update -- sibling reconciliation flows in the same group may already have run by then. See docs/07 section 11.4.

execution_mode.q: What happens if execution_mode is not set on a reconciliation flow?
execution_mode.a: It defaults to `job` -- the flow runs as its own `05_reconciliation_engine.py` job task, exactly as before v1.5.0. This default is deliberate and permanent: several DABs resources already run recon tasks against onboarded rows, so defaulting to `pipeline` would run those flows twice per cycle.

execution_mode.q: What are the only legal values for execution_mode?
execution_mode.a: `job`, `pipeline`, and `pipeline_audit_only` -- any other value fails the allowed-values check in `_validate_reconciliation_flows`. Note the invalid value still falls back to the more restrictive `job` reading for every other mode-conditional check that follows.

execution_mode.q: Is pipeline mode more expensive than job mode?
execution_mode.a: Yes. Every L3/L4 node materializes a real physical copy in UC storage plus an extra DAG step (and a checkpoint for streaming ones), paid on every source since `materialize` defaults to `always` as of v1.7.3. Budget for this when sizing a group with many single-consumer reconciliation sources. See docs/07 section 11.6.

execution_mode.q: Can I use execution_mode pipeline if my source is written by SCD2 or TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD?
execution_mode.a: No -- `pipeline` streams the source to drive the L5 heal pulse, which requires an append-only producer (V-CYC-7). A source produced by `SCD1/SCD2/SCD3/FULL_SNAPSHOT_CDC` or `TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD` into a `materialized_view` is rejected; use `pipeline_audit_only` instead, which reads the source as a batch and registers no heal lane. See docs/07 section 11.7.

flow_step_id.q: What happens if a transformation flow has no flow_step_id?
flow_step_id.a: Onboarding rejects it: `check_string(..., required=True)` reports `transformation_flow[<missing flow_step_id>].flow_step_id: is required but was missing or empty`. Every other error for that flow is labelled with the same placeholder, so fix this first.

flow_step_id.q: Is there a naming convention for flow_step_id, and is it validated?
flow_step_id.a: Only a non-empty string is enforced. The governance skill's convention is `tf_<entity>_<purpose>`; the value becomes the row key of `config.transformation_flow_spec` and the prefix of every input view id (`<flow_step_id>:input:<input_name>`), so keep it short and stable.

flow_step_id.q: Does the choice of flow_step_id affect runtime cost?
flow_step_id.a: Negligible. It is metadata: a MERGE key at onboarding and a label in the pipeline graph. No data path depends on its length or content.

flow_step_id.q: What if two flows in one spec reuse the same flow_step_id?
flow_step_id.a: The validator does not flag duplicate `flow_step_id` values. `upsert_transformation_flow_spec` merges on `t.flow_step_id = s.flow_step_id`, so the second definition silently overwrites the first in the control table and only one flow enters the graph. Treat uniqueness as your responsibility.

governance_tags.column_tags.q: What happens if I don't set governance_tags.column_tags?
governance_tags.column_tags.a: No column-level Unity Catalog tags are applied. This is inert, not an error — `_validate_governance_tags` returns early when `governance_tags` is `None`, and `column_tags` itself is optional.

governance_tags.column_tags.q: Is column_tags a list of {column, tags} objects or a dict keyed by column name?
governance_tags.column_tags.a: A list of objects: `[{"column": "email", "tags": {"pii": "true"}}]`. `_validate_governance_tags` checks `isinstance(column_tags, list)` and errors 'expected a list' otherwise — a dict keyed by column name is not the validated shape, even though it appears that way in some older doc examples.

governance_tags.column_tags.q: Does tagging many columns slow down the pipeline update?
governance_tags.column_tags.a: Negligible impact on the pipeline itself — tags are applied by a separate post-deployment job task (`04_apply_governance_and_egress.py`) via `ALTER TABLE ... SET TAGS`, decoupled from the streaming DAG, not during pipeline execution.

governance_tags.column_tags.q: Why haven't my column tags shown up right after deploying the pipeline?
governance_tags.column_tags.a: Tags are applied post-deployment, after the pipeline update completes successfully, by a dedicated job task — not at onboarding or during the update itself. Also confirm the run-as principal has `APPLY TAG` on the target; without it tags never appear.

governance_tags.column_tags[].column.q: What if the column field is missing inside a column_tags entry?
governance_tags.column_tags[].column.a: Onboarding rejects the flow: `check_string` runs with `required=True`, producing '<entry_path>.column: is required but was missing or empty'.

governance_tags.column_tags[].column.q: Does column need to be the exact physical column name on the target table?
governance_tags.column_tags[].column.a: Yes — it is validated only as a non-empty string, with no cross-check against the actual target schema. A misspelled column name is accepted at onboarding and only surfaces as a failed `ALTER TABLE` at the post-deployment tagging step.

governance_tags.column_tags[].column.q: Is there a limit to how many column_tags entries I can list?
governance_tags.column_tags[].column.a: Not validated — no maximum is enforced. Cost is negligible per entry since tagging happens once, post-deployment, outside the streaming DAG.

governance_tags.column_tags[].column.q: What happens if column names a column that was dropped via target_config.columns_to_exclude?
governance_tags.column_tags[].column.a: Not cross-validated at onboarding. Since `columns_to_exclude` physically drops the column from the target table, the later `ALTER TABLE ... SET TAGS` for that column would fail at the post-deployment tagging step — verify at runtime.

governance_tags.column_tags[].tags.q: What happens if tags is left out of a column_tags entry?
governance_tags.column_tags[].tags.a: Onboarding rejects the flow: `check_dict_of_str` runs with `required=True`, producing '<entry_path>.tags: is required but was missing'.

governance_tags.column_tags[].tags.q: Can a tag value be a number or boolean, like retention: 7?
governance_tags.column_tags[].tags.a: No — `check_dict_of_str` requires every key and value to be a string, erroring 'expected an object of string -> string' otherwise. Write `"7"` as a string, not a bare number.

governance_tags.column_tags[].tags.q: Does having many key-value tags on one column cost anything at runtime?
governance_tags.column_tags[].tags.a: Negligible — tags are applied once via `ALTER TABLE ... SET TAGS` in the post-deployment job task, not evaluated per row.

governance_tags.column_tags[].tags.q: What happens if I typo a tag key, like pii_typ instead of pii_type?
governance_tags.column_tags[].tags.a: Nothing flags it. Per the inspector tip, keys are written verbatim to the `ALTER TABLE SET TAGS` call — a typo becomes a silently-applied but wrongly-named tag, not a validation error.

governance_tags.table_tags.q: What happens if governance_tags.table_tags is not set?
governance_tags.table_tags.a: No table-level Unity Catalog tags are applied; this is inert, not an error, since `table_tags` is optional in `ALLOWED_GOVERNANCE_TAGS_KEYS`.

governance_tags.table_tags.q: Is table_tags a flat object or does it need column-style {key, value} entries?
governance_tags.table_tags.a: A flat string-to-string object, e.g. `{"cost_center": "CC-9041"}` — validated by `check_dict_of_str`, which requires every key and value to be a string, unlike `column_tags` which is a list of objects.

governance_tags.table_tags.q: Is there a runtime cost to setting several table_tags entries?
governance_tags.table_tags.a: Negligible — like column tags, these apply once via `ALTER TABLE ... SET TAGS` in the post-deployment task, outside the pipeline's streaming execution.

governance_tags.table_tags.q: Do table_tags get applied for a sink-type target?
governance_tags.table_tags.a: No — per docs/04 §3, `target_type: "sink"` flows are skipped entirely for tag application (v1.7.5), since a pure sink has no persisted dataset to `ALTER`. A `governance_tags` block on a sink flow is accepted but inert; `external_sink` is not skipped since it materializes a real table first.

logging_config.mismatch_log_capture.q: What happens if logging_config.mismatch_log_capture is never set?
logging_config.mismatch_log_capture.a: It defaults to `false` since v1.7.3 (was `true` through v1.7.2). Omitting it means no `reconciliation_mismatch_log` rows, and in pipeline mode no `recon__*__mismatch` dataset is registered at all. Set it `true` to opt in.

logging_config.mismatch_log_capture.q: Does mismatch_log_capture gate the same rows as run_log_capture?
logging_config.mismatch_log_capture.a: No -- they are independent. `run_log_capture` gates `reconciliation_run_log`/`reconciliation_result` and the `__metrics` dataset; `mismatch_log_capture` gates only `reconciliation_mismatch_log` rows and the `__mismatch` dataset. You can set one true and the other false.

logging_config.mismatch_log_capture.q: Is mismatch_log_capture expensive to turn on for a high-drift table?
logging_config.mismatch_log_capture.a: Its cost scales with mismatch volume, not table size: it writes one `reconciliation_mismatch_log` row per non-MATCHED record with a full `differing_columns_json`, so a flow with heavy VALUE_DRIFT can generate substantial log volume per run -- unlike `run_log_capture`, which is a fixed one-row-per-target cost.

logging_config.mismatch_log_capture.q: If mismatch_log_capture is true but publish_schema is unset in pipeline mode, what happens?
logging_config.mismatch_log_capture.a: Onboarding rejects it: 'run_log_capture/mismatch_log_capture is true but the flow has no publish_schema.' Since v1.7.07 nothing is exported without a `publish_schema`, because the control-table rows are exported from the PUBLISHED `__mismatch` dataset. Set `publish_schema`, or set both capture flags false.

logging_config.run_log_capture.q: What happens if logging_config.run_log_capture is never set?
logging_config.run_log_capture.a: It defaults to `false` since v1.7.3 (it defaulted to `true` through v1.7.2) -- reconciliation is silent by default. Omitting it means no `reconciliation_run_log`/`reconciliation_result` rows, and in pipeline mode the `recon__*__metrics` dataset is not even registered. Set it `true` explicitly to opt in.

logging_config.run_log_capture.q: Is run_log_capture nested inside logging_config or a top-level flow key?
logging_config.run_log_capture.a: Nested: `logging_config.run_log_capture`, a plain boolean. It is not a per-target field -- one value governs the whole flow's run-log writes across all its targets.

logging_config.run_log_capture.q: Does turning run_log_capture on increase reconciliation cost?
logging_config.run_log_capture.a: It adds one published MV (`recon__*__metrics`, exactly one row) and its control-table export row per run in pipeline mode; the cost is negligible since the metrics dataset is a single-row aggregate, not a per-record scan. In job mode it is just an extra log write.

logging_config.run_log_capture.q: What happens if I declare dq_config.rules but run_log_capture resolves false?
logging_config.run_log_capture.a: Onboarding rejects it, since the rules attach to the `__metrics` dataset which would not exist without capture. The error names how the flag got its value (written false, defaulted false, or overridden false) and tells you to set `run_log_capture: true` explicitly, together with `publish_schema`. See docs/07 section 6.

match_keys.q: What happens if match_keys is not provided?
match_keys.a: Onboarding rejects the flow -- `check_list_of_str(flow.get("match_keys"), ..., required=True)` fails, since match_keys is how the engine identifies the same logical record on both sides; there is no default.

match_keys.q: Does the order of columns in match_keys matter?
match_keys.a: Yes -- `__framework_hash_key` preserves the caller's declared key order, so `(a, b)` and `(b, a)` are different keys. Keep the same declared order on both sides of a hash-precomputed comparison, or the hashes will not line up. See docs/07 section 9.

match_keys.q: Does adding more columns to match_keys make the join more expensive?
match_keys.a: No -- match_keys are hashed into a single `__framework_hash_key` column, so the join is always a single-column equi-join regardless of how many key columns you list; a dozen match_keys costs the same at join time as one.

match_keys.q: What happens if match_keys uses a different key than the table's own primary_keys when hash_precomputed is true?
match_keys.a: The stored hashes describe a different question and the comparison is silently wrong -- use `hash_precomputed: false` in that case so the engine recomputes hashes from this flow's own `match_keys` instead of trusting mismatched stored ones. See docs/07 section 9's best-practice table.

publish_schema.q: What happens if I leave publish_schema unset on a pipeline-mode reconciliation flow?
publish_schema.a: Since v1.7.07, absent means publish nothing: the `__metrics`/`__mismatch` datasets are registered as pipeline-scoped temporary tables. A `dq_config` gate still fires, but no `reconciliation_run_log`/`reconciliation_mismatch_log` row can ever be exported. Leave it unset only for a pure gate (dq_config only, both capture flags false).

publish_schema.q: Does publish_schema take a catalog.schema value or just the schema name?
publish_schema.a: Just the schema name, as a plain string -- for example `recon_results`. The catalog is always the hosting pipeline's own; only the schema is configurable. The schema must already exist and be writable by the pipeline's run-as identity, the framework does not create it.

publish_schema.q: Does setting publish_schema add runtime cost beyond the metrics/mismatch materialization?
publish_schema.a: Not beyond what publishing itself costs: the L3/L4 nodes it makes durable (metrics, mismatch, and a healing flow's prepared `_src`/`_tgt`) are real UC-visible tables instead of pipeline-scoped temporaries, so they persist storage and appear in lineage, but no extra join or scan is introduced by the key itself.

publish_schema.q: Why does onboarding reject publish_schema when execution_mode is job?
publish_schema.a: Because a job-mode flow never produces the `recon__<reconciliation_id>__<target_id>__metrics/__mismatch` datasets publish_schema is meant to place -- rejected on presence via `reject_mode_incompatible_keys`. Set `execution_mode` to `pipeline` or `pipeline_audit_only`, or delete the key.

publish_schema.q: Is publish_schema required for a pipeline-mode healing flow (one with append_target_table)?
publish_schema.a: Yes -- rejected as missing: 'execution_mode 'pipeline' with a healing target (append_target_table) requires publish_schema. The L5 heal handler reads the flow's prepared source and healing target back through the metastore (spark.read.table)'. Set publish_schema, or use `pipeline_audit_only` and heal from the job task.

reconciliation_id.q: What happens if I forget to set reconciliation_id on a flow?
reconciliation_id.a: Onboarding rejects the flow. `spec_validator.py::_validate_reconciliation_flows` calls `check_string(..., required=True)` on it, so a missing or empty `reconciliation_id` fails validation before anything else in the flow is checked.

reconciliation_id.q: Does reconciliation_id need to follow any naming pattern like a three-part table name?
reconciliation_id.a: No. It is a free-form string identifier, not a table reference. It is used verbatim to build dataset names such as `recon__<reconciliation_id>__<target_id>__metrics` and as the restartability key for `reconciliation_run_log`, so keep it stable across onboarding re-runs.

reconciliation_id.q: Does changing reconciliation_id have any performance impact?
reconciliation_id.a: None directly. But since it is the restartability key `reconciliation_run_log.source_batch_fingerprint` is checked against, renaming it makes the engine treat the flow as new and loses prior-run fingerprint history, so a batch target cannot short-circuit to `SKIPPED_ALREADY_PROCESSED` on its next run. See docs/07 section 8.

reconciliation_id.q: Can two reconciliation flows in the same spec share a reconciliation_id?
reconciliation_id.a: The validator does not check cross-flow uniqueness of `reconciliation_id` explicitly, but it is the restartability key for `reconciliation_run_log` and the naming key for published `recon__<reconciliation_id>__<target_id>__*` datasets, so two flows sharing one would collide on those dataset names. Keep it unique per flow.

source_config.asn1_codec.q: What error do I get if asn1_codec is left out on an asn1 flow?
source_config.asn1_codec.a: Onboarding rejects it: `source_config.asn1_codec: is required but was missing or empty` (required only when `source_type` is `asn1`).

source_config.asn1_codec.q: Is asn1_codec case-sensitive, and what are the only legal values?
source_config.asn1_codec.a: Yes. Only the lowercase literals `ber` and `der` are accepted (`ALLOWED_ASN1_CODECS`); anything else fails with 'allowed values are [\'ber\', \'der\']'.

source_config.asn1_codec.q: Does choosing ber vs der change decode performance?
source_config.asn1_codec.a: Not documented as a performance differentiator in this framework — both dispatch to the same partition-level `mapInPandas` decoder in `asn1/decoder.py`. Pick the codec matching your telecom module's actual wire encoding; verify at runtime if throughput differs for your payloads.

No direct validator interaction — `asn1_codec` decodes the binary payload after ZIP/gzip extraction, while `member_format` governs the ZIP/gzip container. Both are independently required/optional pieces of the same `source_type: asn1` flow. See docs/02 §4.

source_config.asn1_pdu_name.q: What happens if I don't set asn1_pdu_name for my ASN.1 source?
source_config.asn1_pdu_name.a: It is genuinely optional: an absent value makes the decoder auto-detect the root PDU (`asn1/decoder.py::detect_root_pdu_name` walks the compiled module for the type nothing else references). This was made optional in 0.0.2 specifically so auto-detection is reachable from a spec.

source_config.asn1_pdu_name.q: Does asn1_pdu_name need to match the exact case used in the .asn file?
source_config.asn1_pdu_name.a: It must be a real type name from the compiled `.asn` module (a plain string, type-checked only); match the identifier exactly as declared in the schema file, since it selects a specific PDU rather than pattern-matching one.

source_config.asn1_pdu_name.q: Does supplying asn1_pdu_name explicitly speed up decoding versus auto-detect?
source_config.asn1_pdu_name.a: Not documented as a performance factor — auto-detection walks the compiled module once per partition just like an explicit name would. Supply it only to override detection, not for speed.

source_config.asn1_pdu_name.q: What happens if my ASN.1 module has a root CHOICE instead of a SEQUENCE?
source_config.asn1_pdu_name.a: The PDU must resolve to a top-level `SEQUENCE`, and `CHOICE` is rejected anywhere in that SEQUENCE's member tree, not only at the top. Real telecom modules are usually root-`CHOICE` shaped, so `asn1_pdu_name` must point at the specific SEQUENCE variant you want decoded. See docs/02 §4 'Choosing asn1_pdu_name on a real telecom module'.

source_config.asn1_schema_path.q: What if asn1_schema_path is missing from an asn1 ingestion flow?
source_config.asn1_schema_path.a: Onboarding rejects it: `source_config.asn1_schema_path: is required but was missing or empty` whenever `source_type` is `asn1`.

source_config.asn1_schema_path.q: Does asn1_schema_path have to point at a real .asn file?
source_config.asn1_schema_path.a: Yes — it must be a real `.asn` module definition file; onboarding only checks it is a non-empty string, so a wrong or non-existent path is not caught until the pipeline actually tries to compile the schema at runtime.

source_config.asn1_schema_path.q: Is there a runtime cost to a large or complex .asn schema file?
source_config.asn1_schema_path.a: The framework compiles the ASN.1 schema once per Spark partition via `mapInPandas` (not once per record), which is specifically the optimization that avoids a severe per-record compilation bottleneck. See docs/02 §4 'High-Performance Partitioned Architecture'.

source_config.asn1_schema_path.q: Can asn1_schema_path live on the same Volume as the data path?
source_config.asn1_schema_path.a: There is no rule against it, but keep schema files in a dedicated location (the sample uses `_asn1_schemas/`) — the reader treats `path` as the binary CDR landing directory and `asn1_schema_path` as a separate, single schema file, not something Auto Loader itself scans for new files.

source_config.auto_flatten_all.q: What happens if I leave out auto_flatten_all entirely?
source_config.auto_flatten_all.a: It defaults to `false` per the JSON schema. Combined with an absent `explode_columns`, the source stays a schema-preserving pass-through — nothing is flattened or exploded.

source_config.auto_flatten_all.q: Do I set auto_flatten_all as a JSON boolean or a quoted string?
