A fully qualified `catalog.schema.table`; `{{catalog}}` and `{{env}}` are substituted once at onboarding, `${param}` is substituted on every update. The Spec Builder renders it as a single box, unlike a reconciliation target which is split into three.

source_inputs[].table.q: Is a large table read in full on every update?
source_inputs[].table.a: For a batch binding, yes: the input is a point-in-time snapshot each update. Set `is_streaming: true` on an append-only source to read only new files or rows through a checkpoint.

source_inputs[].table.q: What if the table does not exist yet when I onboard?
source_inputs[].table.a: Onboarding succeeds; the validator tolerates unresolved references because inputs may be produced by this same group. The first pipeline update fails at graph definition if the name never resolves. Check the three-part name and the catalog grant of the pipeline's run-as identity.

source_inputs[].watermark.delay_threshol.q: What if I give event_time_column but no delay_threshold?
source_inputs[].watermark.delay_threshol.a: Onboarding rejects the input: `...watermark.delay_threshold: is required but was missing or empty`. Both halves of a watermark are mandatory.

A Spark interval string passed straight to `withWatermark`, for example `"10 minutes"` or `"2 hours"`. The validator checks only that it is a non-empty string; a malformed interval fails at graph definition.

source_inputs[].watermark.delay_threshol.q: How does the threshold size affect memory?
source_inputs[].watermark.delay_threshol.a: State is retained for at least the threshold: a larger delay keeps more keys in the state store and delays output of late-arriving windows; a smaller one drops late events. Size it to the real lateness of the source.

source_inputs[].watermark.delay_threshol.q: Is the threshold applied when the input is read in batch mode?
source_inputs[].watermark.delay_threshol.a: No. The watermark overlay is skipped unless `is_streaming` is true, so the value is inert on a batch input and no late-event filtering occurs there.

source_inputs[].watermark.event_time_col.q: Can I set delay_threshold without event_time_column?
source_inputs[].watermark.event_time_col.a: No. Once `watermark` is present both keys are required: `...watermark.event_time_column: is required but was missing or empty`. Omit the whole `watermark` object if you do not need one.

source_inputs[].watermark.event_time_col.q: Does the column have to be a TIMESTAMP already?
source_inputs[].watermark.event_time_col.a: No. `transformation/inputs.py` casts it to `timestamp` before `withWatermark`, because Spark requires a real `TimestampType`. A string that does not parse becomes null and the watermark never advances, so prefer a proper timestamp column.

source_inputs[].watermark.event_time_col.q: Does a watermark cost anything on a batch input?
source_inputs[].watermark.event_time_col.a: Nothing useful: `withWatermark` is applied only when `is_streaming` is true (`if is_streaming and event_time_column`). On a batch input the setting is inert.

source_inputs[].watermark.event_time_col.q: When do I actually need a watermark on an input?
source_inputs[].watermark.event_time_col.a: For stateful streaming operations downstream of the input: stream-stream joins, windowed aggregations and deduplication. Without it Spark keeps state for every key forever. Ingestion-side dedup has its own `dedup_watermark` on `source_config`.

source_system.q: What happens if source_system is omitted?
source_system.a: Nothing — it is descriptive metadata that is never validated, per its own purpose text: 'Descriptive metadata — never validated.' It is stored in the control table if supplied.

source_system.q: Is there a required format or enum for source_system?
source_system.a: No — it is free text, e.g. `"SAP_ERP"` or `"excalibur"`; any non-empty string is accepted, with no allowed-values restriction.

source_system.q: Does source_system's value influence pipeline scheduling or routing?
source_system.a: No — it carries no runtime behaviour; it is purely a labeling field for humans and observability/reporting.

They are two independent places a similar concept can be recorded — `source_system` is a dedicated flow-identity field, while `table_tags` can carry an arbitrary key like `source_system` as a free-form governance tag (see docs/16_usecase_implementation_guide.md's example). Setting one does not populate the other.

source_table_name.q: What happens if source_table_name is not filled in?
source_table_name.a: Nothing functional — it is descriptive metadata stored in the control table, with no validation or default beyond being optional.

source_table_name.q: Should source_table_name be a fully qualified three-part name?
source_table_name.a: No — it is free text describing the source object logically (e.g. `example_raw_table`), not a real three-part `catalog.schema.table` reference the engine resolves; it is never cross-checked against `source_config.path`/`source_table`.
None — it is a label only, never read by the reader or DAG-building code.

source_table_name.q: Does source_table_name need to match source_config.source_table for a zerobus flow?
source_table_name.a: No relationship is enforced — `source_table_name` is purely descriptive metadata while `source_config.source_table` is the actual Delta table name the Zerobus reader attaches to; they can differ with no error.

source_type.q: What happens if source_type is missing on an ingestion flow?
source_type.a: Onboarding rejects it: `source_type: is required but was missing or empty` — every ingestion flow must declare one.

source_type.q: Can I still use the old gcs_autoloader value for source_type?
source_type.a: No — the schema's own migration notes record that `source_type: "gcs_autoloader"` was renamed to `"autoloader"`; only `autoloader`, `zerobus`, `asn1` are in `ALLOWED_SOURCE_TYPES` today, so the old spelling fails the allowed-values check.

source_type.q: Does source_type choice affect whether the flow streams or batches?
source_type.a: No — per `docs/12_module_permutation_matrix.md`, `is_streaming` is decided purely by `target_type == "streaming_table"`; all three readers (`read_autoloader_source`, `read_zerobus_source`, `read_asn1_source`) call `spark.readStream` regardless of `source_type`.

source_type.q: Can any source_type feed any target_type?
source_type.a: Yes — the validator enforces `source_type` and `target_type` independently; there is no `source_type` x `target_type` allow-list. The one structural cross-check is that `cdc_load_strategy: SCD3` is rejected on every ingestion flow regardless of `source_type`, since SCD3 only makes sense downstream of a raw ingestion flow. See docs/12 §1.

target_catalog.q: What happens if target_catalog is not set?
target_catalog.a: Onboarding rejects it: `target_catalog: is required but was missing or empty` on both ingestion and transformation flows.

target_catalog.q: Can target_catalog use the {{catalog}} template placeholder?
target_catalog.a: Yes — the sample spec uses `"target_catalog": "{{catalog}}"`, resolved via the same raw-text substitution as `{{env}}` at onboarding time before the document is parsed.

target_catalog.q: Does target_catalog choice affect runtime cost?
target_catalog.a: None directly — it only determines the Unity Catalog namespace the target table registers in; cost is driven by the actual data volume and `target_type`/`cdc_load_strategy`, not the catalog name.

target_catalog.q: Does target_catalog also feed the auto-derived schema_location default?
target_catalog.a: Yes — for `autoloader`/`asn1` sources, an omitted `source_config.schema_location` is auto-derived as `/Volumes/<target_catalog>/landing/_schemas/<target_table>/`, using this same flow's `target_catalog` and `target_table`. See `spec_validator.py`'s schema-location derivation.

target_config.auto_ttl.expire_in_days.q: What happens if I set timestamp_column but leave out expire_in_days?
target_config.auto_ttl.expire_in_days.a: Auto TTL is treated as not configured at all — `build_auto_ttl_kwarg` logs a WARNING and returns `None` when either sub-field is missing; supplying only one half is not a validation error, it just means TTL never applies.

target_config.auto_ttl.expire_in_days.q: Can expire_in_days be 0 to expire rows immediately?
target_config.auto_ttl.expire_in_days.a: No — the schema sets `minimum: 1`, and `_validate_auto_ttl` calls `check_int(..., minimum=1)`. `expire_in_days: 0` is a hard onboarding error, not a valid 'expire everything now' value.

target_config.auto_ttl.expire_in_days.q: Does auto TTL deletion add ongoing overhead to every pipeline run?
target_config.auto_ttl.expire_in_days.a: Not benchmarked in this repo, but it is implemented as a Delta/Lakeflow row-level auto-TTL decorator kwarg (`storage/table_properties.py::build_auto_ttl_kwarg`) rather than an ad hoc DELETE job, so it runs as part of normal table maintenance rather than a separate expensive scan per update.

target_config.auto_ttl.expire_in_days.q: Can I use auto_ttl.expire_in_days together with cdc_load_strategy SCD2?
target_config.auto_ttl.expire_in_days.a: No — `_validate_auto_ttl` hard-errors unless `cdc_load_strategy` is `APPEND` or `TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD`: 'only supported for cdc_load_strategy in [\'APPEND\', \'TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD\']'. On any CDC-dispatched strategy, remove the `auto_ttl` block or handle expiry in a separate maintenance job.

target_config.auto_ttl.timestamp_column.q: What happens if auto_ttl is present but timestamp_column is left blank?
target_config.auto_ttl.timestamp_column.a: Auto TTL is not applied — `build_auto_ttl_kwarg` treats an incomplete block (missing `timestamp_column` or `expire_in_days`) the same as 'not configured', logging a WARNING rather than failing, since skipping TTL has no correctness impact.

target_config.auto_ttl.timestamp_column.q: What column types are valid for auto_ttl.timestamp_column?
target_config.auto_ttl.timestamp_column.a: It must be `DATE`, `TIMESTAMP` or `TIMESTAMP_NTZ` per the inspector tip; `spec_validator.py` only checks it is a non-empty string, so an incompatible column type is caught at pipeline runtime, not onboarding.

target_config.auto_ttl.timestamp_column.q: Does the choice of timestamp_column affect scan cost for TTL expiry?
target_config.auto_ttl.timestamp_column.a: Not documented beyond the general auto-TTL mechanism; a well-indexed/partitioned timestamp column would be the natural choice but this is not enforced or benchmarked here.

target_config.auto_ttl.timestamp_column.q: Can I use auto_ttl.timestamp_column on an SCD1 or SCD2 target?
target_config.auto_ttl.timestamp_column.a: No — same restriction as `expire_in_days`: `_validate_auto_ttl` only allows `APPEND`/`TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD`. Setting it on any CDC-dispatched strategy is a hard onboarding error naming the incompatible strategy.

target_config.capture_technical_metadata.q: What happens if capture_technical_metadata is left unset on a transformation flow?
target_config.capture_technical_metadata.a: Not explicitly defaulted by the validator — the JSON schema notes it is 'conventionally transformation_flows-only ... not actually restricted by the validator'. Omitting it is not the same as `false`; check the runtime default in `ingestion/technical_metadata.py` before relying on either behaviour.

target_config.capture_technical_metadata.q: Is capture_technical_metadata a boolean, or can I pass a string like "true"?
target_config.capture_technical_metadata.a: Strictly boolean — `check_bool` is used, so `"true"` (a string) is rejected; use the JSON literal `true`/`false`.

target_config.capture_technical_metadata.q: Does turning capture_technical_metadata off save meaningful compute?
target_config.capture_technical_metadata.a: Negligible — it only gates whether `__framework_ingestion_timestamp_utc` is added to the row, a single extra column computed once per batch (`current_timestamp()`), not a per-row cost.

target_config.capture_technical_metadata.q: What breaks if I set capture_technical_metadata to false and don't set sequence_by_column?
target_config.capture_technical_metadata.a: Setting it `false` removes the `__framework_ingestion_timestamp_utc` fallback column that `sequence_by_column` defaults to, which then makes `sequence_by_column` effectively mandatory. Per the attribute reference's errors, the pipeline fails naming a missing `__framework_ingestion_timestamp_utc` column if you leave `sequence_by_column` unset in that case.

target_config.cdc_load_strategy.q: What happens if cdc_load_strategy is not set at all?
target_config.cdc_load_strategy.a: Onboarding rejects the flow — `_validate_target_config` calls `check_string(..., required=True)` for `cdc_load_strategy`, so it is mandatory whenever `target_config` is present; there is no implicit default strategy.

target_config.cdc_load_strategy.q: Are the strategy names case-sensitive, e.g. can I write scd2 or Append?
target_config.cdc_load_strategy.a: Yes, case-sensitive uppercase only — the enum is exactly `["APPEND", "TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD", "SCD1", "SCD2", "SCD3", "FULL_SNAPSHOT_CDC"]`; anything else, including lowercase, fails the `allowed_values` check.

target_config.cdc_load_strategy.q: Which cdc_load_strategy is cheapest to run at scale?
target_config.cdc_load_strategy.a: APPEND is cheapest (no merge, pure append). TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD costs scale with full table size regardless of how much changed (docs/03 §2.0). SCD2 is the most expensive to query historically since it retains every version; SCD3 is flagged in docs/03 as having the 'slow recompute' failure mode since it rebuilds from a hidden history table each run.

target_config.cdc_load_strategy.q: Can I use SCD3 on an ingestion flow?
target_config.cdc_load_strategy.a: No — SCD3 is transformation-flows-only, enforced as a hard error at the ingestion-flow level (not inside `_validate_target_config` itself, which accepts the transformation superset). Docs/03 §2.5 confirms it is 'Allowed only in transformation_flows (never in ingestion_flows)'.

target_config.cdc_load_strategy.q: I set partition_columns alongside an SCD2 strategy — why is the table still unpartitioned?
target_config.cdc_load_strategy.a: Partitioning and liquid clustering only take effect for APPEND and TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD. For SCD1/SCD2/SCD3/FULL_SNAPSHOT_CDC, `apply_changes`/`apply_changes_from_snapshot` do not accept `partition_cols`/`cluster_by` at all, so the fields are silently inert, not rejected. See docs/03 §3.

target_config.cdc_operation_column.q: What happens if cdc_operation_column is not set on an SCD1 target?
target_config.cdc_operation_column.a: Deletes never propagate — the target only ever grows. This is a valid, common configuration (a source can have a real primary key with no explicit delete marker); it is not an onboarding error.

target_config.cdc_operation_column.q: Does cdc_operation_column need to match a specific value type like a single character code?
target_config.cdc_operation_column.a: No fixed format — it is validated only as a non-empty column name string. The actual delete-indicating values it carries are declared separately in `cdc_operation_mapping.delete_values`.

target_config.cdc_operation_column.q: Does configuring a delete-marker column add noticeable overhead to the merge?
target_config.cdc_operation_column.a: Negligible — `_build_apply_as_deletes_expr` in `cdc/scd.py` just derives one extra predicate column passed to `dlt.apply_changes`'s native `apply_as_deletes` parameter; it does not add a separate scan or pass.

target_config.cdc_operation_column.q: Can I set cdc_operation_column on an SCD3 target?
target_config.cdc_operation_column.a: No — the validator confirms this is a validation error on SCD3, which has no delete path at all. It is only meaningful for SCD1, SCD2 and FULL_SNAPSHOT_CDC, per `_validate_target_config`'s `strategies_supporting_delete_marker` set.

target_config.cdc_operation_mapping.dele.q: What error do I get if I set cdc_operation_column but leave out delete_values?
target_config.cdc_operation_mapping.dele.a: Onboarding rejects it — `_validate_target_config` requires `cdc_operation_mapping` as a dict (`required=True`) whenever `cdc_operation_column` is set, and within it `check_list_of_str(..., required=True)` for `delete_values`, so one without the other is a hard error.

target_config.cdc_operation_mapping.dele.q: Is delete_values a JSON array or a comma-separated string in the spec?
target_config.cdc_operation_mapping.dele.a: A JSON array of strings, e.g. `["D"]`. Per the inspector tip, the Databricks App UI accepts it as a comma-separated list in the form and serializes it to a JSON array — but the underlying spec attribute itself is always an array.

target_config.cdc_operation_mapping.dele.q: Does listing multiple delete_values slow down the CDC merge?
target_config.cdc_operation_mapping.dele.a: Negligible — it becomes one `isin(...)`-style predicate passed as `apply_as_deletes` to `dlt.apply_changes`, evaluated once per row alongside the merge itself.

target_config.cdc_operation_mapping.dele.q: On FULL_SNAPSHOT_CDC, how does delete_values interact with the snapshot diff?
target_config.cdc_operation_mapping.dele.a: Per the inspector tip, on FULL_SNAPSHOT_CDC flagged rows are filtered out of the snapshot before the diff runs, so they are deleted by absence rather than by an explicit apply_as_deletes predicate — the same end result reached by a different mechanism than SCD1/SCD2.

target_config.columns_to_check.q: What happens if I don't set columns_to_check on an SCD2 flow?
target_config.columns_to_check.a: Every applicable column is compared for change detection. Per docs/03 §2.0, leaving it empty on SCD2 means one volatile source column (a load timestamp, a batch id) can version every row on every run — scope it deliberately.

target_config.columns_to_check.q: Is columns_to_check a list of column names or SQL expressions?
target_config.columns_to_check.a: A plain JSON array of column name strings, validated by `check_list_of_str`. It does not accept SQL expressions.

target_config.columns_to_check.q: Does a narrow columns_to_check list reduce merge cost on SCD1?
target_config.columns_to_check.a: Not the merge cost itself — per the attribute's rationale, on SCD1 it only narrows the change-detection hash basis; the merge is unaffected, so an unchanged row still costs a write. The savings are in avoiding false-positive 'changed' detections, not I/O.

target_config.columns_to_check.q: Is columns_to_check accepted on an APPEND or TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD target?
target_config.columns_to_check.a: No — the validator rules state it is rejected on APPEND, TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD and FULL_SNAPSHOT_CDC. It is meaningful only where a comparison basis exists: SCD1, SCD2 (history scoping) and SCD3 (which requires it to pivot into current_/previous_ column pairs — registration fails without it).

target_config.columns_to_check.q: Can I include an AES-GCM encrypted column in columns_to_check?
target_config.columns_to_check.a: Never do this — AES-GCM uses a random IV, so ciphertext differs every run even when the plaintext hasn't changed, making every row look changed on every run. This is a documented trap, not currently caught by onboarding validation.

target_config.columns_to_exclude.q: What happens if columns_to_exclude is not set on an SCD1 target?
target_config.columns_to_exclude.a: All resolved columns participate in comparison, and nothing is dropped from the target schema via `except_column_list`. This is the default, inert state — no columns are excluded unless you list them.

target_config.columns_to_exclude.q: Is columns_to_exclude a list of column names, same shape as columns_to_check?
target_config.columns_to_exclude.a: Yes — both are plain JSON arrays of strings, validated by `check_list_of_str`. Do not list `primary_keys` or framework technical columns here; they are excluded automatically.

target_config.columns_to_exclude.q: Does excluding columns reduce the size of the target table?
target_config.columns_to_exclude.a: Yes, meaningfully for wide sources — `cdc/scd.py::_build_except_column_list` passes it straight to `dlt.apply_changes`'s native `except_column_list`, which drops those columns from the target's physical schema entirely (per row and per version on SCD2), not just from comparison.

target_config.columns_to_exclude.q: Is columns_to_exclude valid on APPEND or FULL_SNAPSHOT_CDC?
target_config.columns_to_exclude.a: No — `_validate_target_config` only allows it for SCD1, SCD2 and SCD3 (`strategies_supporting_comparison_exclusion`); on any other strategy it is a hard onboarding error: 'only meaningful for cdc_load_strategy in [...]'.

target_config.empty_target_if_source_emp.q: What is the effective default for empty_target_if_source_empty if I don't set it?
target_config.empty_target_if_source_emp.a: Schema default is `false` — but the field is WITHDRAWN with no runtime effect since 2026-08-29 regardless of its value. A zero-row TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD source blanks the target either way; the in-graph guard cannot run because preserving contents would make the target read itself, which Lakeflow rejects as a cycle.

target_config.empty_target_if_source_emp.q: Is empty_target_if_source_empty a boolean or does it take an object like delete_source_after_extract?
target_config.empty_target_if_source_emp.a: A plain boolean (`true`/`false`), validated by `check_bool` — unlike some other withdrawn/legacy fields in this framework, it has no object form.

target_config.empty_target_if_source_emp.q: Does setting this flag add any evaluation cost since it's a no-op?
target_config.empty_target_if_source_emp.a: Negligible — the value is validated at onboarding but never read at runtime; it costs nothing beyond the one-time validation check.

target_config.empty_target_if_source_emp.q: If I set empty_target_if_source_empty to false, is my TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD target protected from a zero-row source?
target_config.empty_target_if_source_emp.a: No. Per docs/03 §2.2 and the documented known errors, the guard has no runtime effect regardless of the value set. Treat every TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD target as unprotected and add a row-count check in a post-update job task outside the pipeline graph instead.

target_config.encrypted_columns.q: What happens if encrypted_columns is absent?
target_config.encrypted_columns.a: Nothing is encrypted; every column is written in clear. `_validate_encrypted_columns` returns when the list is `None`.

target_config.encrypted_columns.q: What shape does each encrypted_columns entry need?
target_config.encrypted_columns.a: An object with `column_name` and `secret` (both required) plus optional `output_column`, `mode` and `source_data_type`. A non-list value is rejected with `expected a list of column configs`.

target_config.encrypted_columns.q: How much does column encryption cost per update?
target_config.encrypted_columns.a: One `aes_encrypt` per row per listed column, plus a cast to string first. Ciphertext is binary and larger than the plaintext, so storage and downstream scans grow slightly. The key is resolved once per flow.

target_config.encrypted_columns.q: Why does an encrypted column make SCD2 create a new version every run?
target_config.encrypted_columns.a: GCM and CBC use a fresh IV per call, so the ciphertext of an unchanged value differs on every write. If the column is in `columns_to_check` (or in a reconciliation's `compare_columns`), every row looks changed. Exclude it via `columns_to_exclude`, or use `ECB` when deterministic ciphertext is acceptable.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].column.a: Yes: `...encrypted_columns[<n>].column_name: is required but was missing or empty`.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].column.q: Should I use the source column name or the post-normalisation name?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].column.a: The name as it exists in the DataFrame when encryption runs, which is after `column_normalization` and standardisation on an ingestion flow. It must also pass `assert_safe_identifier`.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].column.q: Does encrypting a wide column cost more than a narrow one?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].column.a: Yes, linearly with plaintext size: the value is cast to string and enciphered whole. Encrypt the sensitive column only, not a struct that contains it.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].column.q: What if the column is not present at run time?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].column.a: The update fails with `Column '<name>' configured for encryption not present in DataFrame` wrapped in a `CryptoError`. Onboarding cannot see the schema, so a rename upstream surfaces here.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].mode.q: Which AES mode applies when mode is omitted?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].mode.a: `GCM` (`col_config.get("mode", "GCM")`), which also authenticates the ciphertext. The validator only checks the key when it is present.
No. `ALLOWED_AES_MODES = {"GCM", "CBC", "ECB"}` is matched exactly at onboarding; `gcm` is rejected as not an allowed value.
All three are single-pass ciphers; GCM adds a tag computation. The measurable difference is in storage, not CPU: GCM carries a 12-byte IV and a 16-byte tag per value, CBC a 16-byte IV, ECB neither.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].mode.q: When is ECB the right choice despite being deterministic?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].mode.a: When two tables must join on the encrypted value without decrypting, or when the column feeds `columns_to_check`, hashing or reconciliation comparisons: only ECB yields the same ciphertext for the same plaintext. Accept that equal values are visible as equal.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].output.q: Where does the ciphertext go if output_column is not set?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].output.a: It replaces the source column in place: `output_column` defaults to `column_name` in `apply_aes_column_encryption`, and the plaintext is gone from the target.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].output.q: Any restriction on the output column name?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].output.a: It must pass `assert_safe_identifier` at run time; onboarding checks only that it is a string.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].output.q: Does keeping both plaintext and ciphertext columns cost much?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].output.a: One extra binary column per row. The real cost is the security one: the plaintext is still in the table.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].output.q: Which name does the downstream decrypted_columns entry use?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].output.a: This one. The `original_data_type` tag is recorded against `output_column`, and `decrypted_columns[].cast_to_type` is checked against that tag. Point `column_name` on the decrypt side at `output_column` from the encrypt side.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.q: What if secret_catalog is missing on an encrypted column?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.a: `check_secret_ref` reports `...secret.secret_catalog: is required but was missing or empty` and onboarding fails.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.q: Can I pass a classic secret scope here?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.a: No. The reference is a Unity Catalog three-level secret resolved with `dbutils.secrets.get(catalog=, schema=, key=)`; there is no scope form anywhere in the framework.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.q: Is the secret fetched on every row or every micro-batch?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.a: Neither. It is resolved once at graph definition per column config and embedded as a literal in the encryption expression.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.q: Can encryption keys live in a catalog other than the data catalog?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.a: Yes. Many teams keep a dedicated security catalog. The pipeline's run-as identity must be able to read the secret there; onboarding does not check grants.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.q: What happens when secret_key is missing?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.a: Onboarding rejects the column: `...secret.secret_key: is required but was missing or empty`.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.q: What must the secret contain, and is its length validated?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.a: The AES key bytes; Spark's `aes_encrypt` accepts 16, 24 or 32-byte keys. Onboarding validates only the reference, not the key, so a wrong-length key fails at graph definition.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.q: Is a 32-byte key slower than a 16-byte key?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.a: Marginally more rounds per block, not measurable against I/O. Choose the length by policy, not speed.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.q: What happens if I rotate the secret value in place?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.a: New writes use the new key immediately; rows already encrypted with the old key cannot be decrypted by the downstream `decrypted_columns` entry, which fails the consumer's update. Follow the rotation runbook in docs/05 §5 and re-encrypt before switching consumers.
No: `...secret.secret_schema: is required but was missing or empty`.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.q: How should the schema be written?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.a: The bare schema name, unquoted, case as created in Unity Catalog.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.q: Does the schema choice matter for performance?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.a: No; it is part of a single lookup made once per flow.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.q: What if the schema exists but the pipeline cannot read the secret?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].secret.a: Graph definition fails when `dbutils.secrets.get` is denied; onboarding passes because grants are not visible to the validator. Grant the pipeline principal before the first update.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].source.a: No. When omitted the framework records the type Spark observes at encryption time as the `original_data_type` tag, the pre-v1.4.0 behaviour. Declaring it only adds a check.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].source.q: How is the declared type compared with the real one?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].source.a: Case-insensitively and whitespace-trimmed against Spark's reported type string, so `DECIMAL(18,2)` equals `decimal(18,2)`. Onboarding validates only that it is a non-empty string.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].source.q: Does the declaration add run-time cost?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].source.a: None beyond one string comparison per column per update.

target_config.encrypted_columns[].source.q: What does a mismatch look like?
target_config.encrypted_columns[].source.a: The update fails loudly: `encrypted_columns source_data_type mismatch for column '<name>': the spec declares source_data_type='string' but Spark reports 'int'`. That is the point: a silent upstream type change becomes a visible failure instead of a wrong tag that breaks `cast_to_type` downstream.

target_config.generate_hash_columns.q: What is the default for generate_hash_columns if I don't set it on an SCD2 flow?
target_config.generate_hash_columns.a: Defaults to `true` for every CDC-dispatched strategy (SCD1/SCD2/SCD3/FULL_SNAPSHOT_CDC) per docs/03 §4 — `__framework_hash_key` and `__framework_hash_value` are added automatically unless explicitly disabled.

target_config.generate_hash_columns.q: Is generate_hash_columns a boolean or does it accept a list of columns to hash?
target_config.generate_hash_columns.a: A plain boolean, validated by `check_bool`. It only toggles the two fixed columns `__framework_hash_key`/`__framework_hash_value`; which source columns feed the value hash is controlled separately via `columns_to_check`/`columns_to_exclude`.

target_config.generate_hash_columns.q: Does generating hash columns add meaningful compute per row?
target_config.generate_hash_columns.a: A SHA-256 computation per row, over the primary keys and the resolved comparison columns — cheap per row but scales with row count on every run, since both columns are recomputed each update, not incrementally.

target_config.generate_hash_columns.q: What happens if generate_hash_columns is true but no primary_keys are configured?
target_config.generate_hash_columns.a: Both hash columns are skipped with a `WARNING` (docs/03 §4) — but this path is unreachable through normal onboarding, since `primary_keys` is required for every CDC-dispatched strategy; it only fires for a hand-edited control-table row bypassing the validator. Also note: changing `columns_to_check`/`columns_to_exclude` re-hashes every row on the next run, reporting everything as changed once — expected, not a bug.

target_config.liquid_clustering_columns.q: What happens if liquid_clustering_columns is not set?
target_config.liquid_clustering_columns.a: The target table is created with no liquid clustering — behaviourally identical to an explicitly empty list, though no diagnostic log line is emitted for the empty/absent clustering case (unlike `partition_columns`, which does log an INFO when explicitly empty).

target_config.liquid_clustering_columns.q: Can liquid_clustering_columns include more than 3 columns if I really need them?
target_config.liquid_clustering_columns.a: No — capped at 3, Delta Liquid Clustering's own limit. `_validate_target_config` hard-rejects more than `MAX_LIQUID_CLUSTERING_COLUMNS` (3) at onboarding, and `build_partition_and_cluster_kwargs` re-enforces the identical guard at runtime as defense in depth.

target_config.liquid_clustering_columns.q: Is liquid clustering cheaper than partitioning for a large table?
target_config.liquid_clustering_columns.a: For anything under roughly 1 TB, Databricks guidance is to prefer liquid clustering over partitioning — it gives data skipping without the small-file problems partitioning causes, and its clustering keys can be changed later without rewriting the table.

target_config.liquid_clustering_columns.q: Does liquid_clustering_columns take effect on an SCD2 target?
target_config.liquid_clustering_columns.a: No — per docs/03 §3, both `partition_columns` and `liquid_clustering_columns` only take effect for `cdc_load_strategy` in `{APPEND, TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD}`. On SCD1/SCD2/SCD3/FULL_SNAPSHOT_CDC, `apply_changes`/`apply_changes_from_snapshot` do not accept `cluster_by` at all, so the field is silently inert, not rejected.

target_config.partition_columns.q: Is omitting partition_columns different from setting it to an empty array?
target_config.partition_columns.a: Behaviourally identical — both produce an unpartitioned table, since `build_partition_and_cluster_kwargs` never passes an empty list through as `partition_cols=[]` (a zero-column `partitionBy()` has no defined behaviour). They are diagnostically distinct only: an explicitly empty list logs an INFO recording a deliberate opt-out; an omitted field logs nothing.

target_config.partition_columns.q: Is there an alias like partition_by I can use instead of partition_columns?
target_config.partition_columns.a: No — docs/03 §3 is explicit: 'There is no alias: partition_by is not a recognized field name, in this release or any prior one.' Use `target_config.partition_columns` exactly.

target_config.partition_columns.q: Will partitioning a small table improve query performance?
target_config.partition_columns.a: Likely the opposite — Databricks guidance is not to partition tables under roughly 1 TB; use `liquid_clustering_columns` instead. Partitioning on a high-cardinality column like an id produces millions of tiny files, which is a documented failure mode here.

target_config.partition_columns.q: Why does partition_columns appear to have no effect on my SCD1 target?
target_config.partition_columns.a: Partitioning is silently skipped for CDC-dispatched strategies — `apply_changes` does not accept `partition_cols`. This is expected behaviour, not a bug; use APPEND/TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD if you need a partitioned target, or accept an unpartitioned CDC target. See docs/03 §3.

target_config.partition_mode.q: What happens if partition_mode is left unset in the Databricks App form?
target_config.partition_mode.a: It behaves as "absent" — `partition_columns` is omitted from the emitted spec entirely. This attribute is a Databricks App UI-only helper (`server/core/deserializer.py`), not a field the onboarding validator or JSON schema recognizes as a `target_config` key.

target_config.partition_mode.q: Does partition_mode ever get written into the actual onboarding spec JSON?
target_config.partition_mode.a: No — it is a form-only concept with three states (`absent`, `unpartitioned`, `named`) that the app deserializes into the real spec attribute `target_config.partition_columns` (omitted, `[]`, or a named list respectively). Only `partition_columns` reaches `spec_validator.py`.

target_config.partition_mode.q: Does choosing unpartitioned vs absent in partition_mode change runtime cost?
target_config.partition_mode.a: No difference at all — both produce the same emitted spec behaviour (no `partition_cols` kwarg reaches the `@dlt.table` decorator); the distinction is purely diagnostic logging (an INFO line for the explicit `unpartitioned`/empty-list case), not a performance one.

target_config.partition_mode.q: If I pick named in partition_mode but leave the column list empty, what is emitted?
target_config.partition_mode.a: Not directly documented for that exact combination; treat it as equivalent to `unpartitioned` (an empty `partition_columns: []`) since the underlying spec attribute is what actually matters — verify the app's exact deserialization behaviour in `server/core/deserializer.py` if precision matters.

target_config.primary_keys.q: What happens if primary_keys is missing on an SCD1 flow?
target_config.primary_keys.a: Onboarding rejects the flow — `check_list_of_str(..., required=True)` fires for `cdc_load_strategy` in `{SCD1, SCD2, SCD3, FULL_SNAPSHOT_CDC}`. It is not required for APPEND/TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD, which need no key at all.

target_config.primary_keys.q: Should primary_keys be a single string or always a list, even for one column?
target_config.primary_keys.a: Always a JSON array of strings, even for a single-column key: `["customer_id"]`, validated by `check_list_of_str`. A bare string is rejected.

target_config.primary_keys.q: Does a composite (multi-column) primary_keys list cost more at merge time?
target_config.primary_keys.a: Marginally — `apply_changes` matches on the full composite key, and `__framework_hash_key` hashes the ordered keys joined by `||`. Not separately benchmarked here, but a composite key is standard practice for a genuine composite business key, not a performance anti-pattern.

target_config.primary_keys.q: What happens if the declared primary_keys column is renamed by column_normalization before it reaches the target?
target_config.primary_keys.a: This is only caught once the graph executes, not at onboarding — a key that never reaches the clean upstream (renamed by `column_normalization`, or never present in the source, since `data_standardization_sql` can only add/replace columns, never remove them) surfaces as a runtime failure, not a validation error.

target_config.sequence_by_column.q: What sequencer is used if sequence_by_column is not set?
target_config.sequence_by_column.a: Falls back to `__framework_ingestion_timestamp_utc`, which is `current_timestamp()` evaluated once per batch — monotonic and correct across runs, but tied within a single batch, so two versions of the same key in one batch resolve non-deterministically.

target_config.sequence_by_column.q: Can sequence_by_column reference more than one column, like a tie-breaker pair?
target_config.sequence_by_column.a: No — it is a single string column name, validated by `check_string`. There is no composite/multi-column sequencer support in this field.

target_config.sequence_by_column.q: Does declaring a real sequence_by_column add overhead compared to the fallback?
target_config.sequence_by_column.a: Negligible — `apply_changes` always needs some sequencer; supplying a real source column instead of the batch-timestamp fallback costs nothing extra and simply gives a more precise ordering.

target_config.sequence_by_column.q: Does sequence_by_column have any effect on a FULL_SNAPSHOT_CDC flow?
target_config.sequence_by_column.a: No — it is silently discarded. `apply_changes_from_snapshot` has no `sequence_by` parameter at all, so a value here passes validation and is then never read. Also note: setting `capture_technical_metadata` to `false` removes the fallback column, making this field effectively mandatory on APPEND/TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD-style flows that rely on the default sequencer.

target_config.sink_config.export_trigger.q: What happens if I don't set export_trigger on a pgp_zip sink?
target_config.sink_config.export_trigger.a: It defaults to `per_micro_batch`, the only pre-v1.7.5 behaviour: the sink is fed from the flow's own staged view and produces one archive per micro-batch of an append-only stream. This is fine for any genuinely streaming source.

target_config.sink_config.export_trigger.q: Is export_trigger valid on a delta or kafka sink?
target_config.sink_config.export_trigger.a: No. It is presence-rejected for `format` values other than `pgp_zip` with 'only meaningful for format pgp_zip ... whose write cadence Lakeflow itself owns. Remove the attribute.' Only `per_micro_batch` and `per_update` are legal values, and only on a `pgp_zip` sink.

target_config.sink_config.export_trigger.q: Does per_update cost more than per_micro_batch per pipeline run?
target_config.sink_config.export_trigger.a: Negligible extra cost: `per_update` adds one shared `_flowx_export_pulse` dataset (one row, no business data) per pipeline, reused by every `per_update` sink, so N sinks on it are N graph edges, not N streams. The real cost is producing exactly one archive per update regardless of whether new data arrived, which is the intended behaviour for a contractual feed.

target_config.sink_config.export_trigger.q: Why can't I export a materialized_view or TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD target through this sink without export_trigger?
target_config.sink_config.export_trigger.a: A Lakeflow sink is streaming-only, and Delta refuses to stream a table that is fully recomputed each update (`DELTA_SOURCE_TABLE_IGNORE_CHANGES`). Set `export_trigger` to `per_update` so an update-scoped pulse drives the sink while the aggregated rows are read as a batch. See docs/06 'Export trigger'.

target_config.sink_config.export_trigger.q: Will per_update silently skip writing a file when nothing was ingested that update?
target_config.sink_config.export_trigger.a: No, that is the point of `per_update`: it fires even on an update that ingested nothing, so a contractual feed always produces its file. Do not relabel the producing flow as a `streaming_table` to work around the plan-time error instead -- that converts it into a runtime failure.

target_config.sink_config.format.q: What happens if I leave sink_config.format unset?
target_config.sink_config.format.a: Onboarding rejects the flow: `format` is a required key on `sink_config` (`"required": ["format"]` in the schema), and `_validate_sink_config` calls `check_string(..., required=True, allowed_values=ALLOWED_SINK_FORMATS)`. There is no default.

target_config.sink_config.format.q: What are the only legal values for sink_config.format?
target_config.sink_config.format.a: Exactly `delta`, `kafka`, or `pgp_zip` (`ALLOWED_SINK_FORMATS`). Any other value is rejected at onboarding. `delta`/`kafka` dispatch to Lakeflow's own native `dlt.create_sink` formats; `pgp_zip` is this framework's own custom PySpark `DataSource`.

target_config.sink_config.format.q: Is one sink format more expensive at runtime than another?
target_config.sink_config.format.a: Kafka and delta write directly via Lakeflow's native sink writers with no extra staging step. pgp_zip adds a stage-then-archive step per micro-batch (write raw-row files, then zip/gzip and optionally PGP-encrypt them), so it carries more CPU and I/O overhead per batch than the native formats -- proportional to archive size, not a fixed constant.

target_config.sink_config.format.q: Does format decide whether path or kafka_options is required?
target_config.sink_config.format.a: Yes. `kafka` requires `kafka_options` (no filesystem `path` at all); `delta` and `pgp_zip` both require `path` instead. Setting the wrong pairing (e.g. `path` on a `kafka` sink with no `kafka_options`) is rejected at onboarding.

target_config.sink_config.format.q: Does target_type change what format ends up doing?
target_config.sink_config.format.a: Yes. A pure `sink` target skips CDC dispatch entirely -- no main table, no quarantine table -- and the staged view feeds the chosen `format` directly. `external_sink` first materializes a real, governed, DQ-quarantined table and then additionally exports it via a second append flow. See docs/13 K2.

target_config.sink_config.kafka_options.q: What happens if kafka_options is missing on a kafka-format sink?
target_config.sink_config.kafka_options.a: Onboarding rejects the flow. The schema requires `kafka_options` whenever `format == 'kafka'`, and `_validate_sink_config` further hard-errors if `kafka.bootstrap.servers` or `topic` is missing or falsy inside it, even if the key is present as an empty object.

target_config.sink_config.kafka_options.q: Do I write kafka option keys exactly as Spark's Kafka writer expects, like kafka.bootstrap.servers?
target_config.sink_config.kafka_options.a: Yes -- keys are the same flat options a Spark Structured Streaming Kafka writer takes, written verbatim. A typo in a key name is not caught: it becomes a silently ignored option rather than an onboarding error, since `kafka_options` accepts any string-to-string map beyond the two required keys.

target_config.sink_config.kafka_options.q: Does adding more kafka_options entries slow down the sink?
target_config.sink_config.kafka_options.a: Negligible -- these are one-time connection/producer configuration values (batching, compression, security) read once when the Kafka writer is constructed, not per-record processing. Any performance impact comes from the option values themselves (e.g. `linger.ms`, `compression.type`), not the number of keys.

target_config.sink_config.kafka_options.q: How do I put a secret value like a SASL JAAS config into kafka_options without it being a plaintext literal?
target_config.sink_config.kafka_options.a: Use `kafka_secret_options` (option name to a UC secret reference) for an option whose literal value must embed a resolved secret such as `kafka.sasl.jaas.config`; each entry is validated as a required `secret_catalog`/`secret_schema`/`secret_key` reference. Prefer `kafka_options["databricks.serviceCredential"]` when a UC service credential is available instead.

target_config.sink_config.kafka_options.q: Are the secrets I reference from kafka_options resolved lazily when the sink writes?
target_config.sink_config.kafka_options.a: No -- all `sink_config` secrets are resolved eagerly at graph-definition time (Phase 1). If a secret scope or key does not exist, the pipeline fails immediately before any compute starts, not mid-batch. See docs/06 section 3.

target_config.sink_config.path.q: What happens if path is omitted on a delta or pgp_zip sink?
target_config.sink_config.path.a: Onboarding rejects the flow with a required-field error: `path` is mandatory for `format` in `{delta, pgp_zip}` (`check_string(..., required=True)` in `_validate_sink_config`, mirrored by the schema's conditional `required` on `path`). It is not required, and not used, for `kafka`.

target_config.sink_config.path.q: Does path mean the same thing for delta and pgp_zip sinks?
target_config.sink_config.path.a: No -- `path` is the actual Delta table/directory output for `format: delta`, but for `pgp_zip` it is only the per-micro-batch raw-row staging directory (see `archive/pgp_zip_sink.py`), never the finished archive location. The real pgp_zip output lives at `post_export_archive.output_zip_path`. See docs/13 K3.

target_config.sink_config.path.q: Does the choice of path location affect sink throughput?
target_config.sink_config.path.a: Indirectly -- writing staged files (pgp_zip) or Delta files (delta) to a slower storage tier or a heavily-throttled Volume adds I/O latency per micro-batch, same as any Spark writer. The framework applies no extra overhead on top of the underlying storage's own characteristics.

target_config.sink_config.path.q: If I point a downstream consumer at sink_config.path for a pgp_zip sink, will they get the finished archive?
target_config.sink_config.path.a: No -- they will only see the staging area's raw per-partition files, not the archive. Point consumers at `post_export_archive.output_zip_path` instead, which is where the finished ZIP or gzip file actually lands. See docs/13 K3.

target_config.sink_config.path.q: Is path required for a kafka sink even though kafka has no filesystem output?
target_config.sink_config.path.a: No -- `kafka` has no filesystem `path` at all and it is not required; connection details live entirely under `kafka_options` instead.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What archive container do I get if archive_format is left unset?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: It defaults to `zip` -- the unchanged pre-v1.7.4 behaviour: an AES-capable ZIP holding one file per staged partition, with `.zip`/`.zip.pgp` suffixing unaffected.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What file extension does a gzip archive_format actually produce?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: `<export_file_name_format>.<csv|jsonl>.gz`, or `....gz.gpg` when `pgp_encryption` is also enabled -- the suffix is derived from `staged_file_format` so it always matches what is actually inside, e.g. `EE_20260901-LEIDOS_TELEPHONE_001.csv.gz`. A ZIP archive uses `.gpg`/`.pgp` styling instead, never `.gz`.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Is gzip faster or slower than zip for large exports?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Gzip concatenates all staged partition files into a single gzip stream per micro-batch instead of zipping each file separately, which is typically cheaper for a single-recipient text feed since there is no per-file ZIP entry/CRC overhead; both are otherwise a one-time compression pass proportional to export size, not a per-row cost.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Can I still password-protect the archive with post_export_archive.secret if I switch to gzip?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: No -- a gzip stream has no archive password, so `post_export_archive.secret` (an AES password on the ZIP) has no meaning for `gzip`. To protect a gzip export, use `pgp_encryption` instead.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Why does only the first partition's CSV header survive when using gzip with staged_file_format csv?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: A headered CSV writes its header per staged file, and the writer cannot know which partition lands first, so on gzip's single-member concatenation all headers after the first are dropped. This is why `include_header` and `archive_format` interact; JSON-Lines has no header so nothing is dropped there. See docs/06 'Archive container'.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Do I need post_export_archive.enabled if my sink format is pgp_zip?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Yes -- it is required and must be `true` for `pgp_zip`; archiving IS what that sink format does. If `enabled` is present as `false` on a `pgp_zip` sink, onboarding rejects it: 'must be true for format pgp_zip ... use format delta or kafka instead for a sink with no archiving step.'

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Is enabled just a boolean, or does it gate other required fields?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: It is a plain boolean, but when `true` it makes `output_zip_path` required underneath it -- both the schema's conditional `required` and `_validate_sink_config`'s runtime check enforce this together.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does setting post_export_archive.enabled add measurable overhead to every micro-batch?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Yes, but it is inherent to the pgp_zip sink's design, not an optional toggle you can skip while still using that format -- since `enabled` must be `true` for `pgp_zip`, every micro-batch always pays the archive step's cost proportional to the staged data volume.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Can post_export_archive.enabled be set on a delta or kafka sink?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: It is structurally accepted (validated) but unused by the engine for `delta`/`kafka` if a spec author supplies it anyway -- neither native sink format has any concept of a post-write archiving step to hook it up to, so setting it there has no runtime effect.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What happens if post_export_archive itself is omitted entirely on a pgp_zip sink?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Onboarding rejects the flow: `post_export_archive` is required whenever `format == 'pgp_zip'`, with `enabled` required to be `true` inside it -- there is no way to run a pgp_zip sink without archiving.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What file name do I get if export_file_name_format is not set?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: It defaults to `"batch_{batch_id}"`, e.g. `batch_42.zip` -- the framework's pre-existing naming convention (`archive/pgp_zip_sink.py::_render_export_file_name`).

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What placeholders can I actually use inside export_file_name_format?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Only `{batch_id}` (the micro-batch id) and `{timestamp}` (UTC, rendered as `YYYYMMDDTHHMMSSZ` at commit time). Any other placeholder, such as `{export_file_date}` or `{export_file_sequence}`, raises an `ArchiveError`: 'unknown placeholder ... (supported: {batch_id}, {timestamp})' -- this is a runtime error from the sink's `str.format()` call, not caught at onboarding.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does a complex export_file_name_format template slow down each export?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Negligible -- it is a single `str.format()` call per micro-batch commit, not a per-row operation. Choose any literal text plus the two supported placeholders freely.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Do I need to add the .zip or .csv.gz extension myself in export_file_name_format?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: No -- this template renders only the bare file name; the `.zip`/`.zip.pgp` or `.csv.gz`/`.jsonl.gz`(`.gz.gpg`) suffix is always appended by the caller afterwards based on `archive_format`, `staged_file_format` and whether `pgp_encryption` is on. Never encode the archive extension yourself.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Is export_file_name_format validated at onboarding time for bad placeholders?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Not fully -- onboarding only checks it is a string (`check_string`). An unknown placeholder is not rejected at onboarding; it fails at pipeline runtime with `ArchiveError: Invalid export_file_name_format ...: unknown placeholder ...` when the sink actually tries to render a file name.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What happens if I enable post_export_archive but leave output_zip_path blank?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Onboarding rejects the flow: `output_zip_path` is required whenever `enabled` is `true`, both in the schema's conditional `required` and in `_validate_sink_config`'s `check_string(..., required=True)`.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Is output_zip_path the same directory as sink_config.path?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: No -- they should be different directories. `sink_config.path` is the per-micro-batch staging location for a pgp_zip sink, while `output_zip_path` is where the finished archive (ZIP or gzip) is actually written; consumers should read from `output_zip_path`, not `path`. See docs/13 K3.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does the destination volume for output_zip_path affect export latency?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Yes, in the same way any Spark/DBFS write does -- writing the finished archive to a slower storage tier or external Volume with throttling adds I/O latency to the commit step; the framework itself adds no additional overhead beyond the underlying storage write.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Can output_zip_path point at an external partner Volume outside my own catalog?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Yes -- it is just a string path and is commonly an external Volume path (e.g. `/Volumes/{{catalog}}/egress/zips/`) for partner drop zones; the framework does not restrict it to the pipeline's own catalog.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: One output_zip_path, many micro-batches -- do files overwrite each other?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Not by default, because the file name normally includes `{batch_id}` or `{timestamp}` (via `export_file_name_format`), which differs per micro-batch. If you set a static file name with no varying placeholder, later micro-batches will overwrite earlier archives at the same path.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What happens if pgp_encryption block is present but enabled is left out?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Onboarding rejects it: `enabled` is a required key on `pgp_encryption` (`check_bool(..., required=True)` and the schema's `"required": ["enabled"]`). Omit the whole `pgp_encryption` object instead if you don't want PGP encryption at all.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Is pgp_encryption.enabled just a plain boolean like other enabled flags?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Yes -- a plain boolean, but when `true` it makes exactly one of `passphrase_secret` or `recipient_public_key_secret` required underneath it; when `false` (or the object absent) the archive is written unencrypted.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: How much overhead does turning on PGP encryption add per export?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Not negligible but bounded -- it is one additional encryption pass over the finished archive bytes per micro-batch/update, proportional to archive size; it is not a per-row cost and does not affect the staging step itself.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What happens if I set pgp_encryption.enabled true but supply neither passphrase_secret nor recipient_public_key_secret?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Onboarding falls into the asymmetric branch by default and requires `recipient_public_key_secret` (`check_secret_ref(recipient_secret, ..., required=True)` when `passphrase_secret` is absent), so it is rejected as a missing required secret reference.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Can pgp_encryption.enabled be true on a delta or kafka sink's post_export_archive?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: It is structurally accepted if a spec author supplies `post_export_archive` on `delta`/`kafka`, but it is unused by the engine -- neither native sink format has an archiving step to encrypt in the first place.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What happens if pgp_encryption is enabled and I don't set passphrase_secret or recipient_public_key_secret?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Onboarding treats the recipient-key path as required by default and rejects the flow for a missing `recipient_public_key_secret`, since neither secret was supplied. There is no default encryption key -- one of the two must be explicit.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Can I set both passphrase_secret and recipient_public_key_secret at once for extra safety?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: No -- they are mutually exclusive; a PGP message is encrypted either to a recipient key or under a shared passphrase, never both. Onboarding rejects the flow verbatim: 'passphrase_secret (symmetric) and recipient_public_key_secret (asymmetric) are mutually exclusive -- set exactly one.'

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Is symmetric passphrase encryption faster than encrypting to a recipient key?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Not documented as meaningfully different -- both are a single AES256 encryption pass over the archive per micro-batch/update (`crypto/pgp.py::pgp_encrypt_symmetric`); the difference is cryptographic mode (shared secret vs public key), not measured throughput.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Can I sign the export if I use passphrase_secret instead of a recipient key?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: No -- signing (`sign_with_private_key_secret`) requires a sender keypair, which symmetric encryption has none of. Setting `sign_with_private_key_secret` or `sign_passphrase_secret` alongside `passphrase_secret` is rejected: 'signing requires a sender keypair and is not available for symmetric (passphrase_secret) encryption.'

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Since anyone with the passphrase can decrypt, can they also forge a file that looks like it came from us?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Yes -- with symmetric encryption the same secret both encrypts and decrypts, so anyone holding the passphrase can produce an identical, indistinguishable file. Use a recipient key plus a signature (`sign_with_private_key_secret`) wherever the receiver must be able to prove who sent the file. See docs/05 section 4.1.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What happens if I set passphrase_secret but leave out secret_catalog?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Onboarding rejects it: `secret_catalog` is required inside every UC secret reference (`check_string(..., required=True)` in `check_secret_ref`), alongside `secret_schema` and `secret_key`.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does secret_catalog need to match the pipeline's own catalog?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Not necessarily by rule, but conventionally it does -- the sample in docs and UC6's live spec both use `{{catalog}}` (the pipeline's own bundle-variable catalog) so the secret lives alongside the pipeline it serves; there is no validator constraint forcing this.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does resolving secret_catalog at graph-definition time add latency to every pipeline start?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Negligible, a one-time `dbutils.secrets.get(catalog=, schema=, key=)` lookup per sink at Phase 1 graph definition, not a per-micro-batch cost. If the catalog/scope does not exist, the pipeline fails immediately before any compute starts.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Is secret_catalog the Unity Catalog three-level namespace for this key, and does it differ from source_zip_handling's decryption secret catalog?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Yes -- it is the same three-level UC secret reference shape (`secret_catalog`/`secret_schema`/`secret_key`) used identically for every encryption/decryption key, ZIP password, PGP key and Kafka credential in the framework; it is independent of and can differ from the ingest-side `pre_extraction_decryption` secret catalog.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What happens if secret_key is left blank inside passphrase_secret?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Onboarding rejects it: `secret_key` is required and must be a non-empty string inside a secret reference. A missing or empty `secret_key` fails `check_string(..., required=True)`.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does secret_key need any particular naming convention like a prefix?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: No format is enforced beyond being a non-empty string; the framework's own examples use plain descriptive names like `pgpkey` or `pii_encryption_key`. It must match a real key already created via `databricks secrets put-secret`.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does the length or content of the passphrase behind secret_key affect encryption speed?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Negligible -- encryption is AES256 regardless of passphrase content; the passphrase itself only feeds key derivation, not the cost of the encryption pass over the archive.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: If I rotate the secret value behind secret_key, do I need to redeploy the pipeline?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: No redeploy is needed for a value rotation since the reference (catalog/schema/key names) is unchanged and resolution happens fresh at each graph-definition-time run; only changing which secret_key name is referenced requires an onboarding spec change and redeploy.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What if secret_key names a key that does not exist in the given secret_catalog/secret_schema?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Not caught at onboarding -- validation only checks the three fields are non-empty strings. It fails at pipeline graph-definition time (Phase 1) when `dbutils.secrets.get` cannot resolve it, before any compute starts. See docs/06 section 3 and docs/13 S6.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What happens if secret_schema is omitted from passphrase_secret?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Onboarding rejects it: `secret_schema` is required and must be a non-empty string, exactly like `secret_catalog` and `secret_key` in the same `check_secret_ref` call.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Can secret_schema be any schema name, or must it be a schema literally named 'security' or 'config'?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Any schema name is accepted by the validator; the samples use `config` or `security` by convention (UC6 uses `config`, other samples use `security`), but nothing enforces a particular schema name.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does putting the secret in a dedicated schema change lookup performance?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Negligible -- it is one `dbutils.secrets.get` call at graph-definition time regardless of which schema the secret lives in; schema choice is an organizational/governance decision, not a performance one.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Who needs grants on secret_catalog.secret_schema to onboard and run this flow?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Not documented in the validator or docs/06/13 read for this group -- the code only validates the reference shape, not permissions. Grounding is thin here: verify the required UC secret-scope grant (e.g. `USE SCHEMA`/`SELECT` equivalent on the secret) at deploy/runtime rather than assuming a default.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What happens if enabled is true and recipient_public_key_secret has no secret_catalog?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Onboarding rejects it: `secret_catalog` is required inside the secret reference, and `recipient_public_key_secret` itself is required whenever `passphrase_secret` is absent and `enabled` is `true`.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Is secret_catalog for the recipient key the same catalog as the sink's own output path?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Not required to be -- it is only a UC secret lookup location, independent of `sink_config.path`/`output_zip_path`. Samples commonly use `{{catalog}}` for convenience, but any catalog holding the secret works.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Is resolving a recipient public key more expensive than a passphrase secret?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Negligible -- both are the same single `dbutils.secrets.get` call at graph-definition time; the difference is the cryptographic operation performed afterward (asymmetric vs symmetric), not the secret lookup cost.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Can I use recipient_public_key_secret together with sign_with_private_key_secret for signed asymmetric export?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Yes -- signing is only available in the asymmetric (`recipient_public_key_secret`) mode, since it requires a sender keypair; `sign_with_private_key_secret` is exactly for this combination and is rejected only when paired with `passphrase_secret` instead.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What happens if I set enabled true, recipient_public_key_secret object present, but secret_key missing?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Onboarding rejects it: `secret_key` is required and must be a non-empty string, same as every other secret reference field validated by `check_secret_ref`.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does secret_key here need to reference a public key specifically, not a private key?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: The framework does not validate key content at onboarding -- it only validates the reference shape. You must put the recipient's actual PGP public key material behind this `secret_key`; using the wrong key type is not caught until decryption/encryption actually runs.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does key size (2048 vs 4096-bit RSA) behind secret_key affect export runtime noticeably?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Not documented; likely a small, bounded per-archive cost difference from asymmetric key operations, but no measurement is given in docs/05 or docs/06. Treat as negligible relative to the archive's own I/O and compression cost unless observed otherwise.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What error do I get if secret_key names a key that does not exist in Unity Catalog?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Not validated at onboarding -- it fails at pipeline graph-definition time (Phase 1) when the secret cannot be resolved, before any compute starts. See docs/06 section 3 and docs/13 S6 for why resolution happens eagerly outside the sink's own worker process.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What happens if secret_schema is left out of recipient_public_key_secret?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Onboarding rejects it: `secret_schema` is required and must be a non-empty string, alongside `secret_catalog` and `secret_key`, in the same `check_secret_ref` validation.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Do secret_catalog, secret_schema and secret_key together form a three-level namespace like a table reference?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Yes -- it is resolved via `dbutils.secrets.get(catalog=, schema=, key=)`, structurally the same three-level namespace used for every encryption/decryption key, ZIP password, PGP key and Kafka credential in the framework.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does grouping many partner keys under one secret_schema slow down secret resolution?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Negligible -- each lookup is an independent, one-time `dbutils.secrets.get` call at graph-definition time; the number of other secrets sharing the same schema does not affect resolution cost.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: If I rename the secret_schema without updating the spec, does the pipeline still deploy?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: It deploys (onboarding only checks the string is non-empty) but fails at graph-definition time when the old schema name can no longer be resolved -- not validated at onboarding, fails at pipeline runtime with a secret-resolution error. Update the spec's `secret_schema` to match before redeploying.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What happens if I set sign_passphrase_secret without also setting sign_with_private_key_secret?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Onboarding rejects it: 'sign_passphrase_secret: only meaningful alongside sign_with_private_key_secret, but that field is not set.' It is optional even when the signing key IS set -- an unprotected signing key is a valid configuration too.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does secret_catalog here follow the same three-level shape as the other PGP secret fields?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Yes -- identical `secret_catalog`/`secret_schema`/`secret_key` shape, validated the same way via `check_secret_ref`, resolved via `dbutils.secrets.get(catalog=, schema=, key=)`.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does adding a signing passphrase on top of encryption noticeably slow down export commits?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Negligible -- it is one additional secret lookup at graph-definition time plus unlocking the signing key during the encryption pass, not a per-row cost.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Can sign_passphrase_secret be used with passphrase_secret (symmetric encryption) instead of a recipient key?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: No -- signing is asymmetric-only. Any signing field, including `sign_passphrase_secret`, set alongside `passphrase_secret` is rejected: 'signing requires a sender keypair and is not available for symmetric (passphrase_secret) encryption.'

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: If sign_with_private_key_secret is set but sign_passphrase_secret's secret_key is left out, does signing still work?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Yes -- `sign_passphrase_secret` is entirely optional even when `sign_with_private_key_secret` is set, since an unprotected signing private key is a valid configuration. Only when `sign_passphrase_secret` is present is it required to have all three fields, including `secret_key`, filled in.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Is secret_key here the passphrase that protects the signing key itself, not the signing key value?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Yes -- this secret reference points to the passphrase that unlocks the private signing key referenced by `sign_with_private_key_secret`; it is a different secret from the signing key material itself.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does unlocking a passphrase-protected signing key add noticeable latency versus an unprotected one?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Not documented with a measurement; expect a small, one-time key-unlock cost during the signing step, negligible relative to archive compression and encryption.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What happens if the value behind this secret_key does not actually match the signing key's passphrase?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Not validated at onboarding -- the reference shape is checked, not the passphrase's correctness. A mismatch fails at pipeline runtime when the sink attempts to unlock and use the signing key, not before.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Is sign_passphrase_secret.secret_schema required if I only set sign_with_private_key_secret and no sign_passphrase_secret at all?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: No -- the whole `sign_passphrase_secret` object, including `secret_schema`, is optional and only validated when the object is present at all. Omit it entirely for an unprotected signing key.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Can secret_schema for the signing passphrase live in a different schema than the signing key itself?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Yes -- each secret reference (`sign_with_private_key_secret`, `sign_passphrase_secret`) is resolved independently with its own `secret_catalog`/`secret_schema`/`secret_key`, so they can point at different schemas if needed.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does the schema chosen for sign_passphrase_secret affect pipeline startup time?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Negligible -- it is one more independent secret lookup at graph-definition time regardless of which schema it lives in.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What error appears if sign_passphrase_secret is fully specified but sign_with_private_key_secret is absent?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Onboarding rejects the flow verbatim: 'sign_passphrase_secret: only meaningful alongside sign_with_private_key_secret, but that field is not set.' Add the signing key reference or remove `sign_passphrase_secret` entirely.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What happens if I want a signed export but leave out sign_with_private_key_secret entirely?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: No error -- signing is fully optional. `pgp_encryption` proceeds unsigned (recipient-key encryption only) when neither `sign_with_private_key_secret` nor `sign_passphrase_secret` is set.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does secret_catalog for the signing key need to be the same catalog as recipient_public_key_secret?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Not required -- each secret reference is resolved independently; the signing key and the recipient's public key can live in different catalogs/schemas.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does adding a digital signature meaningfully slow down the export compared to encryption alone?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Adds one signing operation per archive on top of encryption, a bounded cost proportional to archive size -- not documented with a specific number here, but structurally it is one extra crypto pass, not a per-row cost.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Can I set sign_with_private_key_secret when using passphrase_secret (symmetric) encryption?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: No -- rejected. Signing requires a sender keypair, which symmetric encryption has none of; setting `sign_with_private_key_secret` alongside `passphrase_secret` triggers: 'signing requires a sender keypair and is not available for symmetric (passphrase_secret) encryption.'

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: If sign_with_private_key_secret object is present but secret_key is blank, what happens?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Onboarding rejects it: `secret_key` is required and must be a non-empty string, same as every field inside a `check_secret_ref`-validated object.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does secret_key here reference the private signing key material itself, not a public key?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Yes -- this is the sender's private key used to sign the export, distinct from `recipient_public_key_secret` (the recipient's public key used to encrypt). The framework does not validate key content, only that the reference resolves to a string.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Is there extra overhead from using a large RSA signing key here?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Not measured; expect a bounded per-archive signing cost from the asymmetric operation itself, negligible relative to compression and I/O for typical export sizes.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What happens at runtime if the value behind secret_key is not actually a valid PGP private key?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Not validated at onboarding -- only the reference shape is checked. An invalid key fails at pipeline graph-definition time when the sink resolves and attempts to use it for signing, before any data moves (see docs/13 S6 on why resolution happens outside the sink's worker process).
