target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Is secret_schema required if I only set enabled true with a recipient key and no signing at all?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: No -- the entire `sign_with_private_key_secret` object is optional; when absent, no signing is attempted and none of its sub-fields, including `secret_schema`, are validated.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Should the signing key's secret_schema match the encryption key's secret_schema for consistency?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Not required by the validator -- each is an independent three-level UC secret reference; organizing them in the same schema is a convention, not a rule.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does resolving both an encryption key and a signing key from different schemas add noticeable latency?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Negligible -- both are one-time `dbutils.secrets.get` lookups at graph-definition time (Phase 1), done once per pipeline deployment, not per micro-batch.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Can sign_with_private_key_secret's secret_schema be reused across multiple sinks in the same pipeline?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Yes -- there is no per-sink uniqueness constraint on secret references; the same catalog/schema/key can be referenced by multiple sinks that need to sign with the same organizational key.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What happens if post_export_archive.secret is set for AES password protection but secret_catalog is missing?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Onboarding rejects it: `secret_catalog` is required inside `secret` just like any other `check_secret_ref`-validated object, via `check_secret_ref(archive_config.get("secret"), ...)`.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Is post_export_archive.secret the same three-level shape as pgp_encryption's secrets?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Yes -- identical `secret_catalog`/`secret_schema`/`secret_key` shape, resolved the same way via `dbutils.secrets.get`. It is a separate, independent password: an AES password on the ZIP itself, not a PGP key.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does adding a ZIP password via secret slow down archive creation?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Negligible -- one additional secret lookup at graph-definition time; the AES-password ZIP write itself is comparable in cost to an unencrypted ZIP write of the same size.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Can I combine post_export_archive.secret with pgp_encryption at the same time?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Yes -- the ZIP password (`secret`) is independent of, and combinable with, `pgp_encryption`; you get an AES-password-protected ZIP that is then also PGP-encrypted. This combination has no meaning under `archive_format: gzip`, since a gzip stream has no archive password at all.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What happens if secret.secret_key is left out while secret.secret_catalog and secret_schema are set?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Onboarding rejects it: `secret_key` is required and must be a non-empty string, same as every field validated by `check_secret_ref`.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Is the value behind this secret_key the ZIP password itself?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Yes -- it is the AES password applied to the ZIP archive (independent of any PGP key), resolved via `dbutils.secrets.get` and never written as a literal into the spec, control tables or logs.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does the ZIP password length affect archive write performance?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Not documented with a measurement here; AES-capable ZIP encryption cost scales with archive size, not passphrase length, so any effect from password length itself should be negligible.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does secret.secret_key apply when archive_format is gzip?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: No -- `secret` (an AES password on the ZIP) has no meaning for `gzip`, since a gzip stream carries no archive password at all. Use `pgp_encryption` to protect a gzip export instead.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: What happens if secret.secret_schema is missing while enabling the ZIP password?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Onboarding rejects it: `secret_schema` is required and must be a non-empty string inside `secret`, validated the same way as `secret_catalog` and `secret_key`.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Can secret.secret_schema be the same schema as the pgp_encryption keys, or must it be separate?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Either works -- there is no constraint tying `post_export_archive.secret`'s schema to `pgp_encryption`'s; they are independently resolved three-level secret references and can share or differ in schema freely.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: Does resolving the ZIP password secret add to pipeline startup time alongside the PGP secrets?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: Negligible -- one more `dbutils.secrets.get` call at graph-definition time (Phase 1), same cost class as any other secret reference in `sink_config`.

target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.q: If secret is fully specified but archive_format is gzip, does onboarding warn me it will be ignored?
target_config.sink_config.post_export_ar.a: `_validate_sink_config` validates `secret` unconditionally whenever present, with no check against `archive_format`. Not validated at onboarding; it silently has no effect at runtime for `gzip` per docs/06's 'Archive container' note. Verify at runtime rather than assuming a rejection.

target_config.sink_config.staged_file_fo.q: What staged file shape do I get inside the archive if staged_file_format is left unset?
target_config.sink_config.staged_file_fo.a: It defaults to `json` -- JSON-Lines, one JSON object per row, the only pre-v1.6.0 behaviour. Non-JSON-native values (dates, decimals, binary) are stringified rather than failing the micro-batch.

target_config.sink_config.staged_file_fo.q: Can I use staged_file_format on a delta or kafka sink to control its output shape?
target_config.sink_config.staged_file_fo.a: No -- it is presence-rejected there: 'only meaningful for format pgp_zip ...; format "delta"/"kafka" is a native Lakeflow sink with no staging step. Remove the attribute.' It only applies to `pgp_zip`.

target_config.sink_config.staged_file_fo.q: Is csv staging more expensive than json staging per micro-batch?
target_config.sink_config.staged_file_fo.a: Not quantified in docs/06, but structurally csv writes one file per non-empty partition with its own header row versus JSON-Lines' one-object-per-row stream; both are a single pass over the micro-batch's rows, so any difference should be negligible relative to archive compression and I/O.

target_config.sink_config.staged_file_fo.q: Does csv staged_file_format interact with archive_format gzip in a way I should know about?
target_config.sink_config.staged_file_fo.a: Yes -- because a headered CSV writes its header per staged file and gzip concatenates all staged files into one stream, every header after the first is dropped on concatenation. JSON-Lines has no header, so nothing is lost there. See docs/06 'Archive container'.

target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.q: What field separator do I get in the staged CSV if delimiter is not set?
target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.a: It defaults to `,` (comma) -- Python's csv `excel` dialect, the pre-v1.7.4 behaviour, when `staged_file_options` (or just `delimiter`) is omitted.

target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.q: Can I use a multi-character delimiter like || for a pipe-pair separated feed?
target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.a: No -- it must be exactly one character. Onboarding rejects a multi-character value verbatim: 'must be exactly one character, got \'||\' -- Python's csv writer cannot emit a multi-character delimiter.'

target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.q: Does choosing a non-comma delimiter like | affect write throughput?
target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.a: Negligible -- the delimiter is just a single character passed to Python's csv writer dialect; it has no measurable effect on staging throughput regardless of which single character is chosen.

target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.q: Is delimiter valid if staged_file_format is left at the json default?
target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.a: No -- `staged_file_options` (and therefore `delimiter`) only applies when `staged_file_format == 'csv'`; JSON-Lines has no delimiter concept, and setting it otherwise is rejected: 'only meaningful when staged_file_format == csv (JSON-Lines staging has no delimiter or header row).'

target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.q: What happens downstream if a field value itself contains the delimiter character?
target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.a: The writer quotes such fields per RFC-4180, so a value containing the delimiter is still correctly delimited -- but confirm the receiving consumer actually honours CSV quoting rather than naively splitting on the delimiter character.

target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.q: If I don't set include_header, does the staged CSV get a header row?
target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.a: Yes -- it defaults to `true`. Omitting the attribute is not the same as setting it `false`; you must explicitly set `false` to suppress the header for a headerless supplier interface.

target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.q: Is include_header meaningful for a JSON-Lines staged file?
target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.a: No -- like `delimiter` and `line_terminator`, it is only meaningful when `staged_file_format == 'csv'`; JSON-Lines has no header row concept and setting `staged_file_options` there is rejected.

target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.q: Does turning off include_header measurably speed up export writes?
target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.a: Negligible -- writing or skipping one header row per staged partition file has no measurable effect on overall micro-batch throughput.

target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.q: If include_header is true and archive_format is gzip, do I get one header per row group or one for the whole file?
target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.a: You get one header written per staged partition file, but since gzip concatenates all staged files into a single stream, only the first file's header survives -- every subsequent header is dropped during concatenation. This is a direct interaction between `include_header` and `archive_format`; see docs/06 'Archive container'.

target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.q: What line ending does the staged CSV use if line_terminator is left unset?
target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.a: It defaults to `crlf` -- RFC-4180 style, and the pre-v1.7.4 behaviour, matching legacy mainframe/Windows interface expectations.

target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.q: Why is line_terminator spelled as crlf or lf instead of a literal control character?
target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.a: Because a JSON string cannot carry a bare control character unambiguously and reliably survive round-tripping, so it is spelled as a name (`"crlf"`/`"lf"`) rather than embedding a literal `\r\n` or `\n` in the spec.

target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.q: Does the choice between crlf and lf affect write performance?
target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.a: Negligible -- it only changes which two-or-one-byte sequence terminates each row; there is no measurable throughput difference between the two.

target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.q: My Unix consumer reports a stray \r at the end of every row -- what setting fixes this?
target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.a: Set `line_terminator` to `lf`. The default `crlf` leaves a trailing `\r` before the `\n` on each row, which a consumer that splits on `\n` only will see as a stray carriage return at the end of the last field.

target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.q: Does line_terminator apply if staged_file_format is json?
target_config.sink_config.staged_file_op.a: No -- like `delimiter` and `include_header`, it is only valid alongside `staged_file_format: 'csv'`; JSON-Lines staging has no configurable line terminator concept in this validator path.

target_config.sink_config.write_mode.q: What write behaviour do I get for a delta sink if write_mode is left unset?
target_config.sink_config.write_mode.a: Always append, regardless of whether `write_mode` is set at all -- `@dlt.append_flow` (the mechanism every sink uses) is inherently append-only. Omitting it changes nothing.

target_config.sink_config.write_mode.q: What values does write_mode accept, and does setting overwrite actually overwrite the sink?
target_config.sink_config.write_mode.a: Only `overwrite` or `append` (`ALLOWED_SINK_WRITE_MODES`) pass onboarding validation, but per the schema's own `$comment`, this is a dead field: it validates fine but is never read by the engine's `delta` sink branch, so setting `overwrite` has no effect -- the sink still only appends.

target_config.sink_config.write_mode.q: Does setting write_mode to overwrite reduce storage growth on the sink target?
target_config.sink_config.write_mode.a: No -- since the value is never read by the engine, setting `overwrite` has zero effect on runtime behaviour or storage growth; the sink always appends regardless of this attribute.

target_config.sink_config.write_mode.q: Should I still include write_mode in new specs for documentation purposes?
target_config.sink_config.write_mode.a: No -- the schema explicitly says to omit it in real specs ('Kept here only for fidelity with the validator's own constant; omit it in real specs'). It is retained purely so the schema matches the validator's allowed-values constant, not as a meaningful configuration knob.

target_config.storage_format.q: What is the target table format if storage_format is not set?
target_config.storage_format.a: The schema declares no default; the physical table is always Delta regardless — `storage_format: "iceberg"` itself is implemented as the UniForm read-compatibility property, since Lakeflow has no separate native-Iceberg storage engine. Treat `delta` as the safe assumption when omitted.

target_config.storage_format.q: Are delta and iceberg the only accepted values, case-sensitive?
target_config.storage_format.a: Yes — `ALLOWED_STORAGE_FORMATS = {"delta", "iceberg"}` (lowercase), checked via `check_string(..., allowed_values=...)`. `"Iceberg"` or `"Delta"` would be rejected.

target_config.storage_format.q: Does setting storage_format to iceberg add overhead versus plain delta?
target_config.storage_format.a: Not separately benchmarked here; it enables IcebergCompat properties (UniForm) so both Delta and Iceberg readers can read the table, which has some write-side metadata overhead versus plain Delta, but this repo does not quantify it.

target_config.storage_format.q: Can I set storage_format: iceberg on a streaming_table or materialized_view target?
target_config.storage_format.a: No — `_validate_target_config` hard-errors: 'iceberg is only valid when target_type == batch_table'. For any other target_type, leave `storage_format` on `delta` and instead set `table_properties.enable_iceberg_read_uniformity: true`, which achieves Iceberg read compatibility via UniForm without changing `storage_format`.

target_config.table_properties.q: What happens if table_properties is not set at all?
target_config.table_properties.a: No custom Delta table properties are applied — `_validate_table_properties` returns immediately when the value is `None`. Log retention, VACUUM windows and Iceberg-read-uniformity all stay at their platform defaults.

target_config.table_properties.q: Are table_properties values like log_retention_duration strings or numbers?
target_config.table_properties.a: Always strings, even for a duration like `"interval 30 days"` — `check_string` is used for both `log_retention_duration` and `deleted_file_retention_duration`. `enable_iceberg_read_uniformity` is the one key validated as a real boolean via `check_bool`, not a string `"true"`.

target_config.table_properties.q: Does raising log_retention_duration or deleted_file_retention_duration cost storage?
target_config.table_properties.a: Yes, directly — a longer retention window keeps more Delta log versions and unreferenced data files around (for time-travel and safe concurrent reads), which increases storage footprint proportionally to the retention period and table churn rate.

target_config.table_properties.q: What happens if I set deleted_file_retention_duration too low for a long-running query?
target_config.table_properties.a: VACUUM can remove files still being read by that query, causing a `FileNotFoundException` mid-query, per the documented known error. Raise `deleted_file_retention_duration` above your longest expected query duration to avoid this.

target_configs.q: What happens if target_configs is left empty or missing?
target_configs.a: Onboarding rejects the flow: 'is required and must be a non-empty list of target objects' -- a reconciliation flow needs at least one target to compare the source against.

target_configs.q: Is target_configs a single object or an array?
target_configs.a: An array of objects -- one flow can compare its source against multiple, independently-configured targets. Each entry becomes one object in a JSON array; a wholly blank entry is dropped on save.

target_configs.q: Does adding more entries to target_configs multiply the reconciliation cost?
target_configs.a: Yes, roughly linearly -- each `target_configs[]` entry gets its own L3 prepared-target node and L4 classify/metrics/mismatch nodes, so N targets means N independent full outer joins against the shared source, each materializing its own set of datasets.

target_configs.q: Must every target_configs[] entry use the same read_mode as the source?
target_configs.a: Not necessarily the same, but constrained: at most one side of a given target's comparison may be streaming (source_config or that target_configs[] entry, never both), because a stream-stream join only supports inner/left_outer semantics and cannot express the framework's full four-way classification.

target_configs[].append_target_table.a: Only when `comparison_direction` is `source_to_target` or `both` (the default) -- `check_string(..., required=True)` fires in that branch. With `comparison_direction: target_to_source` alone, it can be omitted since nothing is ever appended in that direction.

target_configs[].append_target_table.q: Does append_target_table need to already exist before onboarding?
target_configs[].append_target_table.a: Yes -- it must pre-exist. `spark.catalog.tableExists` is unusable in the graph-execution context and creating it on demand would race sibling flows, so a table created on the fly would also miss any `CLUSTER BY (__framework_hash_key)` clustering. See docs/07 section 11.6.

target_configs[].append_target_table.q: Is the append into append_target_table an update-in-place or insert-only?
target_configs[].append_target_table.a: Insert-only -- a drifted record is re-appended as a correction, not updated in place, consistent with the append-only CDC/Zerobus model these targets are typically built on. A restartability fingerprint check prevents duplicate corrections on an unchanged batch source.

target_configs[].append_target_table.q: What happens if append_target_table equals this flow's own source_config.table or another target's table?
target_configs[].append_target_table.a: It is rejected as an append-loop hazard (V-CYC-2/3/5): must not equal this group's own ingestion/transformation target, this flow's own source, or another target_configs[] entry's table -- in pipeline modes this is a hard onboarding error, in job mode it is a warning since there is no live graph to race. See docs/07 section 11.8.

target_configs[].comparison_direction.q: What is the default for comparison_direction if I don't set it?
target_configs[].comparison_direction.a: `both` -- the validator resolves `target_config.get("comparison_direction", "both")` when deciding whether `append_target_table` is required, and the JSON schema documents the same default.

target_configs[].comparison_direction.q: What are the legal values for comparison_direction?
target_configs[].comparison_direction.a: `source_to_target`, `target_to_source`, or `both` -- `ALLOWED_COMPARISON_DIRECTIONS`; any other string fails the allowed-values check.

target_configs[].comparison_direction.q: Does comparison_direction change how much work the join does?
target_configs[].comparison_direction.a: No -- `matcher.py::match_reconciliation_target` always computes all four classification categories in one full outer join regardless of `comparison_direction`; computing all four is effectively free once the join has run. What it gates is action (append vs. audit-only), not classification cost.

target_configs[].comparison_direction.q: Does target_to_source ever write corrections back anywhere?
target_configs[].comparison_direction.a: No -- `target_to_source`/`both` only mismatch-logs MISSING_IN_SOURCE records for audit; this direction never appends and never mutates the target. Nothing in the module is permitted to delete or modify a target based on a MISSING_IN_SOURCE finding. See docs/07 section 8.

target_configs[].data_standardization_sq.q: What happens if data_standardization_sql is not set on a target_configs entry?
target_configs[].data_standardization_sq.a: No cleanup is applied -- the target's columns are used as read (after filter_condition), unmodified, going into matching.

The same restricted single-column-expression grammar as ingestion: each entry must be one column expression ending in `AS <column_name>` (e.g. `trim(status) AS status`), must not contain `;`, and must not contain a full SELECT/FROM/JOIN/UNION statement -- `_validate_standardization_expression` rejects any of those. Entered as a comma-separated list in the UI, stored as a JSON array of strings.

target_configs[].data_standardization_sq.q: Is data_standardization_sql expensive to run on a large target?
target_configs[].data_standardization_sq.a: Negligible per-entry -- each is a simple column-level expression (trim, cast, etc.) evaluated once per row during the read pass, not a join or aggregation; cost scales linearly with row count and number of expressions, same as any projection.

target_configs[].data_standardization_sq.q: Does data_standardization_sql run before or after filter_condition on a target?
target_configs[].data_standardization_sq.a: After -- it is applied last, following filter_condition, per docs/07 section 3.2's per-side field ordering. It also runs before hashing, so standardized values (not raw ones) feed into the __framework_hash_value computation when hash_precomputed is false.

target_configs[].filter_condition.q: What happens if filter_condition is left unset on a target_configs entry?
target_configs[].filter_condition.a: No filter is applied after the read -- the full table (after any task_run_id_column narrowing) is used for matching. No default value is substituted.

target_configs[].filter_condition.q: Does target_configs[].filter_condition support ${param} substitution the same way as elsewhere?
target_configs[].filter_condition.a: Yes -- it supports `${param}` substitution, resolved against the owning dataflow group's `pipeline_parameters` on every pipeline update. Do not wrap the placeholder in quotes yourself for a string parameter: `substitute_dynamic_parameters` already supplies the quotes, so `load_date = '${run_date}'` becomes `load_date = ''2024-01-01''`, a ParseException. Write `load_date = ${run_date}` instead.
Yes -- it is applied after the read but before matching, so a selective filter reduces the row count that reaches the hash-key join and the Phase 1/2 fingerprint computation for that side.

target_configs[].filter_condition.q: In what order is target_configs[].filter_condition applied relative to task_run_id_column and data_standardization_sql?
target_configs[].filter_condition.a: Task_run_id_column narrowing applies first (immediately after read), then filter_condition, then data_standardization_sql last. A filter_condition can narrow an already task_run_id-narrowed set further, but never widen it. See docs/07 section 5.2.

target_configs[].hash_precomputed.q: What is the default for hash_precomputed on a target_configs entry?
target_configs[].hash_precomputed.a: `false` -- same default as on `source_config`: the engine computes `__framework_hash_key`/`__framework_hash_value` now from this target's raw (post-standardization) columns rather than trusting stored ones.

target_configs[].hash_precomputed.q: Is hash_precomputed valid on every target_configs entry regardless of type?
target_configs[].hash_precomputed.a: It is valid because reconciliation targets are always `type: table` -- but onboarding still rejects `hash_precomputed: true` if that entry's `type` is somehow not `table`, since only a framework-managed table can carry pre-built hash columns.

target_configs[].hash_precomputed.q: Does setting hash_precomputed true on a target save more than on the source?
target_configs[].hash_precomputed.a: The saving is symmetric per side -- each side that sets it true skips its own hash computation pass. For a large target this is often the bigger win, since targets are frequently the larger, already-materialized dataset in the comparison.

target_configs[].hash_precomputed.q: What if hash_precomputed is true on the target but the upstream CDC flow that wrote it didn't enable generate_hash_columns?
target_configs[].hash_precomputed.a: It fails at runtime, not onboarding, with a hard error naming the missing columns: 'hash_precomputed=True but dataset is missing [__framework_hash_key, __framework_hash_value] -- this dataset was not actually produced by a CDC-dispatched flow with generate_hash_columns enabled'. See docs/07 section 9.

target_configs[].read_mode.q: What is the default for a target's read_mode?
target_configs[].read_mode.a: `batch` -- same default as `source_config.read_mode`; `ALLOWED_READ_MODES = {"batch", "streaming"}` and the sample spec shows `"read_mode": "batch"` as the norm.

target_configs[].read_mode.q: Are the legal values for target read_mode the same as for the source?
target_configs[].read_mode.a: Yes -- `batch` or `streaming`, validated by the same `_validate_reconciliation_dataset_config` function that handles both `source_config` and each `target_configs[]` entry.

target_configs[].read_mode.q: Is a streaming target read cheaper than a batch one?
target_configs[].read_mode.a: Not inherently cheaper -- it trades a full table scan for incremental micro-batch reads plus checkpoint state, which helps for a large append-only target read repeatedly but adds checkpoint management overhead a plain batch read does not need.

target_configs[].read_mode.q: Can source read_mode be batch while a target's read_mode is streaming?
target_configs[].read_mode.a: Yes, in job mode -- one flow can freely mix a streaming source against a batch target or vice versa, as long as at most one side of a given target's comparison is streaming (a stream-stream join is unsupported). In `pipeline`/`pipeline_audit_only` mode, `streaming` is rejected on presence for every side.

target_configs[].target_catalog.q: What happens if target_catalog is not set on a target_configs entry?
target_configs[].target_catalog.a: Onboarding rejects it as required -- it is composed with `target_schema`/`target_table` into the three-part table name the target side reads, so it cannot be left out.

target_configs[].target_catalog.q: Can target_catalog use the {{catalog}} template variable?
target_configs[].target_catalog.a: Yes -- the sample spec shows `"target_catalog": "{{catalog}}"`, resolved at onboarding time the same way `{{catalog}}`/`{{env}}` resolve elsewhere in the spec.

target_configs[].target_catalog.q: Does target_catalog choice affect reconciliation cost?
target_configs[].target_catalog.a: Negligible directly -- it only participates in composing the fully-qualified table name. Cross-catalog reads have the same cost profile as same-catalog reads in Unity Catalog; the actual cost driver is the target table's row count and whether hash_precomputed avoids a re-hash.

target_configs[].target_catalog.q: Is target_catalog required even when comparison_direction is target_to_source only?
target_configs[].target_catalog.a: Yes -- it, along with target_schema/target_table, identifies the dataset to read for this side regardless of comparison_direction; comparison_direction only gates what action is taken on the classification, not whether the target is read at all.

target_configs[].target_id.q: What happens if target_id is missing on a target_configs entry?
target_configs[].target_id.a: Onboarding rejects it -- `check_string(target_id, ..., required=True)` fails; every target needs an identifier for logging and dataset naming.

target_configs[].target_id.q: Can target_id repeat across two entries in the same flow's target_configs?
target_configs[].target_id.a: No -- the validator tracks `seen_target_ids` and rejects a duplicate: 'target_id must be unique within a reconciliation flow', naming the earlier index it collides with.

target_configs[].target_id.q: Does the value chosen for target_id affect performance?
target_configs[].target_id.a: No -- it is purely an identifier used in log rows and in the published dataset names `recon__<reconciliation_id>__<target_id>__metrics`/`__mismatch`; it carries no runtime cost of its own.

target_configs[].target_id.q: Where does target_id show up in the published datasets?
target_configs[].target_id.a: It is embedded in every L3/L4 node name for that target, e.g. `_recon__<rid>__<tid>__tgt`, `recon__<rid>__<tid>__metrics`, `recon__<rid>__<tid>__mismatch`, and in `reconciliation_run_log`/`reconciliation_mismatch_log` rows to identify which target a row belongs to. See docs/07 section 11.1's L0-L5 node map.

target_configs[].target_schema.q: What happens if target_schema is left out of a target_configs entry?
target_configs[].target_schema.a: Onboarding rejects it as required -- like `target_catalog` and `target_table`, it is composed into the three-part table name on save and there is no default.

The docs show `{{catalog}}`/`{{env}}` template variables supported on related string fields such as `target_catalog`/`filter_condition`; `target_schema` is a plain string field composed the same way, e.g. `"bronze_example"` in the sample.

target_configs[].target_schema.q: Does target_schema choice have a performance effect?
target_configs[].target_schema.a: No direct effect -- it is purely part of the fully-qualified table identity used to read the target. Cost is driven by the target table's size and read pattern, not its schema name.

target_configs[].target_schema.q: Does target_schema participate in the append-loop V-CYC checks?
target_configs[].target_schema.a: Indirectly, yes -- `target_catalog.target_schema.target_table` together form the qualified reference the V-CYC placement checks (V-CYC-2/3/5) compare against `append_target_table` and other in-spec targets to detect append-loop hazards. See spec_validator.py's `_validate_reconciliation_pipeline_placement`.

target_configs[].target_table.q: What happens if target_table is missing on a target_configs entry?
target_configs[].target_table.a: Onboarding rejects it as required -- composed with `target_catalog`/`target_schema` into the three-part name this target side reads; there is no default and no way to reconcile against an unnamed table.

target_configs[].target_table.q: Is target_table just the bare table name?
target_configs[].target_table.a: Yes -- a plain string like `example_raw_final`; it is combined with `target_catalog` and `target_schema` to form the fully-qualified `catalog.schema.table` read reference, not a pre-qualified name itself.

target_configs[].target_table.q: Does target_table's row count matter for reconciliation runtime?
target_configs[].target_table.a: Yes -- it directly drives the L3 prepared-target scan and the L4 full outer join cost; a large target benefits most from `hash_precomputed: true` (when the precondition holds) to skip a full re-hash pass.

target_configs[].target_table.q: Can target_table be the same table as this flow's own source_config.table?
target_configs[].target_table.a: As the target itself, no rule forbids that directly, but the composed reference participates in append-loop checks against `append_target_table` (V-CYC-5 and the target_configs[] self/cross-append checks) -- a target's own table must not equal `append_target_table` on the same or another entry, since that would re-arm every future run against its own output.

target_configs[].task_run_id_column.q: What if task_run_id_column is not set on a target_configs entry?
target_configs[].task_run_id_column.a: That target side's read stays correlation-only for `task_run_id` -- no narrowing filter is applied, same backward-compatible behaviour as the source-side default.

target_configs[].task_run_id_column.q: Does target_configs[].task_run_id_column need a specific column name?
target_configs[].task_run_id_column.a: No fixed name is enforced -- any existing column on that target table works. The framework's own tables typically carry `__framework_pipeline_run_id`, which is the conventional value to use.

target_configs[].task_run_id_column.q: Does setting task_run_id_column on a target reduce read cost?
target_configs[].task_run_id_column.a: Yes, when the `task_run_id` job parameter is set -- the target's read is narrowed to that run's rows before `filter_condition` applies, reducing rows scanned in downstream matching for that side.

target_configs[].task_run_id_column.q: Is task_run_id_column allowed on a target when execution_mode is pipeline_audit_only?
target_configs[].task_run_id_column.a: No -- rejected on presence in both pipeline modes, for the same reason as on `source_config`: no stable per-update key exists inside a Lakeflow update, so the narrowing would be a silent no-op. Use `filter_condition` instead.

target_schema.q: What error appears if target_schema is left blank?
target_schema.a: Onboarding rejects it: `target_schema: is required but was missing or empty`, on both ingestion and transformation flows.

target_schema.q: Is there a naming convention target_schema should follow, like bronze_ prefix?
target_schema.a: Not enforced by the validator — it is just a non-empty string. The sample spec uses a `bronze_example` convention, but this is a project convention, not a validated rule.

target_schema.q: Does target_schema's name affect pipeline performance?
target_schema.a: None — it only determines the Unity Catalog schema namespace for the target table; no runtime cost is tied to the name itself.

target_schema.q: Can target_schema differ between an ingestion flow and its downstream transformation flow?
target_schema.a: Yes — nothing forces them to match; a transformation flow references its upstream via `source_inputs[].table` (a fully-qualified name), which can point at any catalog/schema/table combination regardless of this flow's own `target_schema`.

target_table.q: What happens if target_table is omitted?
target_table.a: Onboarding rejects it: `target_table: is required but was missing or empty`, on both ingestion and transformation flows.

target_table.q: Does target_table need to be a bare name or fully qualified?
target_table.a: A bare table name — it is combined with `target_catalog`/`target_schema` elsewhere (e.g. `_qualified_or_none`) to build the fully-qualified reference; do not put dots in it.

target_table.q: Does the target_table name affect performance?
target_table.a: None — it only names the registered Lakeflow dataset; performance is governed by `target_type`, `cdc_load_strategy`, partitioning/clustering, and data volume, not the table name.

target_table.q: Does target_table feed the auto-derived schema_location path?
target_table.a: Yes — for `autoloader`/`asn1` sources with no explicit `schema_location`, the loader derives `/Volumes/<target_catalog>/landing/_schemas/<target_table>/` using this flow's own `target_catalog` and `target_table`. Renaming `target_table` later without moving the schema location will point at the wrong path.

target_type.q: What happens if target_type is missing?
target_type.a: Onboarding rejects it: `target_type: is required but was missing or empty`, on both ingestion and transformation flows — there is no implicit default.

target_type.q: What are the only legal values for target_type?
target_type.a: `streaming_table`, `materialized_view`, `batch_table`, `external_sink`, `sink` (`ALLOWED_TARGET_TYPES`); any other value fails the allowed-values check from `check_string`.

target_type.q: Does materialized_view cost more than streaming_table at runtime?
target_type.a: Yes — `materialized_view` is fully recomputed on every update (not incrementally maintained), so it should be paired with `TRUNCATE_AND_LOAD`, not a CDC strategy; `streaming_table` is the default for incremental, lower-cost ingestion. See the attribute reference's tips and docs/13 line 963.

target_type.q: Can I set storage_format: iceberg with target_type: streaming_table?
target_type.a: No — onboarding rejects it: 'iceberg' is only valid when `target_type == 'batch_table'`. Elsewhere, use `table_properties.enable_iceberg_read_uniformity` with `storage_format: delta` instead. Also note `target_type: sink` bypasses CDC dispatch entirely — `cdc_load_strategy` is never read for a pure sink target. See docs/13 K2 and docs/12 §1.

transform_sql.q: What happens if transform_sql is not set?
transform_sql.a: No reshaping happens -- the missing/drifted record set is appended into `append_target_table` using its own schema as read from `_reconciliation_unmatched_records`, unmodified. Only needed when source and target schemas differ.

transform_sql.q: What must transform_sql select from, and what grammar does it accept?
transform_sql.a: It must read FROM `_reconciliation_unmatched_records` and is full Spark SQL, not the restricted single-expression grammar `data_standardization_sql` uses -- it legitimately needs a complete SELECT/FROM since it reshapes a miss set. It supports `{{catalog}}`/`{{env}}` template variables and is syntax/plan-validated live via EXPLAIN, same as `transformation_sql`.

transform_sql.q: Does transform_sql add meaningful overhead to the append?
transform_sql.a: It adds one extra transform pass over the miss set only (not the full source/target tables), so cost scales with the number of missing/drifted records, which is typically small relative to the compared datasets.

transform_sql.q: Can transform_sql use ${param} placeholders the same way filter_condition does?
transform_sql.a: The doc groups it with filter_condition as supporting `{{catalog}}`/`{{env}}` template resolution at onboarding time; as with any parameterized SQL in this framework, do not wrap a `${param}` placeholder in quotes for a string parameter -- `substitute_dynamic_parameters` already supplies them, and double-quoting causes a ParseException. Write `${param}` bare in the expression.

transformation_sql.q: Can a transformation flow work without transformation_sql?
transformation_sql.a: No. It is `required=True`: `transformation_flow[<id>].transformation_sql: is required but was missing or empty`. A pass-through flow still needs a `SELECT * FROM <input_name>`.

transformation_sql.q: How should I write ${param} placeholders inside transformation_sql?
transformation_sql.a: Bare, never inside your own quotes. `substitute_dynamic_parameters` renders a string parameter as a single-quoted SQL literal, so `WHERE country = '${filter_country}'` becomes `''US''` and fails with a `ParseException`. Write `WHERE country = ${filter_country}`. A placeholder with no matching `pipeline_parameters` key fails onboarding naming the parameter.

transformation_sql.q: Is transformation_sql executed during onboarding, and how heavy is that?
transformation_sql.a: Only an `EXPLAIN` of the post-substitution SQL runs, never the query itself. A `ParseException` is a hard error; structural planning errors (`NUM_COLUMNS_MISMATCH`, `INCOMPATIBLE_COLUMN_TYPE`, typically a misaligned `UNION`) are hard errors; unresolved table references are tolerated because input views exist only at pipeline run time.

transformation_sql.q: Why does my SQL pass onboarding but fail with an unresolved table at pipeline start?
transformation_sql.a: The `EXPLAIN` check deliberately tolerates unresolved references, since `FROM <input_name>` resolves only inside the running graph. At run time a name must match a `source_inputs[].input_name` in the same spec or a fully qualified table. A typo in the alias is therefore caught by the pipeline, not by onboarding.

two_tier_verification.q: What is the effect of not setting two_tier_verification at all?
two_tier_verification.a: It defaults to `true`. A cheap Phase 1 per-side fingerprint (row_count plus an XOR-fold of `__framework_hash_key`/`__framework_hash_value`) runs first and short-circuits the whole comparison when both sides agree; the full hash-key join runs only when Phase 1 disagrees. See docs/07 section 4.

two_tier_verification.q: Is two_tier_verification a per-target setting or per-flow?
two_tier_verification.a: Per-flow -- it is a top-level boolean on the reconciliation flow object, not nested under `source_config` or `target_configs[]`. It applies uniformly to every target this flow compares.

two_tier_verification.q: Does two_tier_verification true make reconciliation cheaper?
two_tier_verification.a: Yes when the sides genuinely agree -- Phase 1 is shuffle-free (one `.agg()` scan, no join) and skips the full outer join entirely on a match. Setting it `false` always runs Phase 2 and pays the join cost on every run, which is only worth it if you cannot tolerate Phase 1's accepted false-equal edge case.

two_tier_verification.q: Can two_tier_verification produce a wrong reconciliation result?
two_tier_verification.a: It can produce a false 'equal' but never a false 'different': the XOR fold cancels in pairs, so two datasets differing by an even number of identical duplicate rows can fold to the same digest. `row_count` in the fingerprint catches every cardinality difference, so this only matters for the narrow same-cardinality, even-multiplicity case. Set it `false` if that risk is unacceptable. See docs/07 section 4.
